stops.caption: The Italian comics monthly named after Linus van Pelt, which opened its first issue in April 1965 with Eco, Elio Vittorini and Oreste del Buono discussing Peanuts. Eco's 1963 introduction to Charlie Brown is the classic statement of why the strip mattered.

source.label: Linus, first issue, April 1965 (Milano Libri)

quote.text: Charlie Brown: ingenuous, stubborn, always awkward, and doomed to failure. … His solitude becomes an abyss, his inferiority complex is pervasive—tinged by the constant suspicion (which the reader also comes to share) that Charlie Brown is not inferior. Worse: he is absolutely normal.
quote.attribution: Umberto Eco, 'On Krazy Kat and Peanuts', The New York Review of Books (13 June 1985; from Apocalittici e integrati, 1964)

stops.title: Linus, the Eco issue
stops.caption: Linus marked Eco's death in 2016 with a back cover drawn as a tribute, Eco as Superman, as Charlie Brown, as a Smurf, and a strip inside. His daughter Carlotta shows it in Davide Ferrario's film.

source.label: Carlotta Eco in Davide Ferrario's film Umberto Eco: La biblioteca del mondo (2022)

quote.text: Ti ricordi questo numero di Linus che hanno fatto una controcopertina, cioè lui vestito da Superman, da Charlie Brown, da Puffo … E poi c'era dentro un fumetto che racconta la storia di come lui guarda dal balconcino praticamente il funerale, e si commuove.
quote.translation: Do you remember this issue of Linus? They did a back cover with him dressed as Superman, as Charlie Brown, as a Smurf. And inside there was a comic strip telling the story of how he watches, more or less, his own funeral from the little balcony, and is moved.
quote.attribution: Carlotta Eco, in Davide Ferrario's film Umberto Eco: La biblioteca del mondo (2022)

stops.title: Corriere dei Piccoli
stops.caption: The children's weekly of the Corriere della Sera, founded in 1908, which printed American strips with the balloons removed and rhyming couplets underneath. It is the paper the amnesiac hero of The Mysterious Flame of Queen Loana finds in the attic, and the one Eco read as a boy.

source.label: askanews, 'I libri e lo Studiolo di Umberto Eco, meraviglie alla Braidense' (5 May 2022)

image.alt: Cover of the first Corriere dei Piccoli, 27 December 1908

stops.title: Topolino giornalista
stops.caption: The 1930s Italian album of the Mickey Mouse strip in which Mickey runs a newspaper, one of the childhood comics Eco gave back to Yambo, the bookseller who has lost his memory in The Mysterious Flame of Queen Loana.

source.label: askanews, 'I libri e lo Studiolo di Umberto Eco, meraviglie alla Braidense' (5 May 2022)

stops.title: Alex Raymond, Flash Gordon
stops.caption: Flash Gordon on the planet Mongo, fighting the tyrant Ming: in The Mysterious Flame of Queen Loana Eco makes him the hero who taught an Italian boy under Fascism what a fight for freedom looked like. Eco also noted, as a collector, what an original Raymond page costs today.

source.label: Biblioteca Universitaria di Bologna, the record of Eco's copy

quote.text: If you want to buy an original of one of the great comic strips, it is horribly expensive, because they are so rare (these days, a single page of Alex Raymond's work costs a fortune). But why are they so rare? Simply because the newspapers that used to publish them threw the plates in the bin the moment the strip had been printed.
quote.attribution: Umberto Eco in conversation with Jean-Claude Carrière, This Is Not the End of the Book (2009; English translation 2011)

stops.title: E. C. Segar, Braccio di Ferro (Popeye)
stops.caption: Popeye, who first walked into Segar's Thimble Theatre in January 1929 and took it over. Eco described himself as a fan and collector of the strips of the 1930s, and Popeye is one of them.

source.label: Biblioteca Universitaria di Bologna, the record of Eco's copy

quote.text: As a fan and collector of 1930s comic strips, I find it quite impossible to read contemporary graphic novels, or at least the most avant-garde. But it's important not to bury one's head in the sand.
quote.attribution: Umberto Eco in conversation with Jean-Claude Carrière, This Is Not the End of the Book (2009; English translation 2011)

image.alt: Popeye's first appearance in Thimble Theatre, 17 January 1929

stops.title: Lee Falk, Mandrake
stops.caption: Mandrake the Magician, the top-hatted hypnotist of 1934, in the pile with the other albums of Eco's childhood.

source.label: askanews, 'I libri e lo Studiolo di Umberto Eco, meraviglie alla Braidense' (5 May 2022)

stops.title: Lee Falk, L'Uomo Mascherato (The Phantom)
stops.caption: The Phantom, the ghost who walks, chasing Diana Palmer through the jungle of Bengalla. Eco counted the Phantom's adventures among the memories he had stolen from books, which he said had given him a very long childhood.

source.label: Umberto Eco: La biblioteca del mondo (Davide Ferrario, 2022)

quote.text: Ho la sensazione di aver avuto un'infanzia lunghissima e piena proprio perché è piena di ricordi che ho rubato ad altri: li ho rubati a Sandokan e Yanez mentre correvano coi loro prao i mari malesi, a D'Artagnan mentre duellava con il barone Winter, all'Uomo Mascherato che inseguiva Diana Palmer, e anche a Renzo e Lucia in fuga sul ramo di Como.
quote.translation: I have the feeling of having had a very long and full childhood, precisely because it is full of memories I stole from others: I stole them from Sandokan and Yanez racing their praus across the Malay seas, from d'Artagnan duelling with Baron Winter, from the Phantom chasing Diana Palmer, and from Renzo and Lucia too, fleeing along the Como branch of the lake.
quote.attribution: Umberto Eco, in Davide Ferrario's film Umberto Eco: La biblioteca del mondo (2022)

stops.title: Tex Willer
stops.caption: The Bonelli western that has run since 1948, the longest-lived Italian comic. Eco kept the studies of it with the strips themselves.

source.label: Biblioteca Universitaria di Bologna, the record of Eco's copy

stops.title: Gianni Brunoro, Corto come un romanzo
stops.caption: A study of Hugo Pratt's sailor Corto Maltese, the most literary of Italian comics heroes. Eco's often-repeated line about Pratt turned the usual snobbery inside out.

source.label: Biblioteca Universitaria di Bologna, the record of Eco's copy

quote.text: Quando ho voglia di rilassarmi leggo un saggio di Engels, se invece desidero impegnarmi leggo Corto Maltese.
quote.translation: When I want to relax I read an essay by Engels; when instead I want something demanding I read Corto Maltese.
quote.attribution: Umberto Eco, as quoted by Marco Pellitteri, 'La nona arte secondo Umberto Eco', doppiozero (2019)

stops.title: Guido Crepax: Valentina, la forma del tempo
stops.caption: Crepax's Valentina, the Milan photographer with the Louise Brooks bob who first appeared in Linus in 1965, in the catalogue of a 2008 exhibition. Crepax and Eco belonged to the same Milan of the 1960s, and Linus was where they met on the page.

source.label: Biblioteca Universitaria di Bologna, the record of Eco's copy

stops.title: Jules Feiffer, Il complesso facile
stops.caption: The Village Voice cartoonist's anxious New Yorkers, in Italian, from 1962: the kind of adult comic strip Linus was founded to publish three years later.

source.label: Biblioteca Universitaria di Bologna, the record of Eco's copy

stops.title: Bonvi, Fall-out fall-out fall-out
stops.caption: Bonvi, the creator of the Sturmtruppen, on life after the bomb. The Italian comic of the 1970s and 1980s, from Linus to the satirical weeklies, is shelved here in the living room.

source.label: Biblioteca Universitaria di Bologna, the record of Eco's copy

stops.title: Nuvole maliziose: fumetti e peccati capitali
stops.caption: Comics and the seven deadly sins, an anthology from 1985. The living-room shelves mix the strips with the books that take them apart.

source.label: Biblioteca Universitaria di Bologna, the record of Eco's copy

stops.title: Annie Baron-Carvais, La bande dessinée
stops.caption: A pocket history of the comic strip in the Que sais-je? series, from the Yellow Kid of 1895 onwards. Eco's own history of the medium was written a generation earlier, essay by essay.

source.label: Biblioteca Universitaria di Bologna, the record of Eco's copy

image.alt: The Yellow Kid by R. F. Outcault (1897)

stops.title: Bertrand Portevin, Le monde inconnu d'Hergé
stops.caption: A study of the hidden world of Tintin's creator. Hergé's clear line belongs to the same 1930s that produced Eco's favourite American strips.

source.label: Biblioteca Universitaria di Bologna, the record of Eco's copy

stops.title: I fumetti di Mao (1971)
stops.caption: Chinese comics of the Cultural Revolution, collected by a journalist in China, with essays by Eco and the sinologist Jean Chesneaux. Eco later remembered how little the comics revealed of what was actually happening.

source.label: Umberto Eco, introduction to I fumetti di Mao (1971)

quote.text: In 1971 I contributed to a book about Chinese comics. A journalist based in China had collected together all kinds of material: comic books in the English style, but also photo stories. The comics had been created during the Cultural Revolution, but they gave no indication whatsoever of what was happening in China at the time.
quote.attribution: Umberto Eco in conversation with Jean-Claude Carrière, This Is Not the End of the Book (2009; English translation 2011)

stops.title: Storia del racconto popolare: prima del fumetto
stops.caption: A history of popular storytelling before the comic strip, from the broadsheet ballad to the illustrated feuilleton, shelved where the serial novels turn into comics.

source.label: Umberto Eco: La biblioteca del mondo (Davide Ferrario, 2022)

stops.title: Umberto Eco, La bustina di Minerva (2000)
stops.caption: Fifteen years of Eco's back-page column in L'Espresso, named after the matchbook he jotted ideas on. The column of June 1991 explained why reading lengthens life.

source.label: Umberto Eco, La bustina di Minerva (2000)

quote.text: Il libro è un'assicurazione sulla vita, una piccola anticipazione di immortalità. All'indietro (ahimé) anziché in avanti.
quote.translation: The book is a life-insurance policy, a small advance on immortality. Backwards, alas, rather than forwards.
quote.attribution: Umberto Eco, 'Perché i libri allungano la vita', La bustina di Minerva, L'Espresso (2 June 1991)

tours.title: Feuilletons and the pleasures of popular fiction
tours.blurb: Eco's first books were the unbound serial novels in his grandfather's box: Dumas, Sue, Salgari. He read them all his life, wrote a book about their supermen, and built The Prague Cemetery out of their engravings. This tour runs along the shelves of popular fiction in the corridor and living room.

stops.title: Umberto Eco, Il superuomo di massa (1976)
stops.caption: The superman of the masses: Eco's book on the heroes of the popular novel, from Sue's Rodolphe and Dumas's Monte Cristo to James Bond, and on the consolations these books provide.

source.label: Umberto Eco, Il superuomo di massa (1976; enlarged 1978)

quote.text: Metterà in opera una tale energia, sprigionerà una tale felicità, se non inventiva almeno combinatoria, da procurare piaceri che sarebbe ipocrita nascondere.
quote.translation: It will set in motion such energy, will release such happiness, if not inventive then at least combinatory, as to procure pleasures it would be hypocritical to hide.
quote.attribution: Umberto Eco, Il superuomo di massa (1978)

stops.title: Emilio Salgari, Le Tigri di Mompracem
stops.caption: Sandokan, the Tiger of Malaysia, and his Portuguese friend Yanez, on the prau against the British of Labuan. Salgari never left Italy; Eco, who read him as a boy in wartime, said the memories were his own.

source.label: Umberto Eco: La biblioteca del mondo (Davide Ferrario, 2022)

quote.text: Ho la sensazione di aver avuto un'infanzia lunghissima e piena proprio perché è piena di ricordi che ho rubato ad altri: li ho rubati a Sandokan e Yanez mentre correvano coi loro prao i mari malesi.
quote.translation: I have the feeling of having had a very long and full childhood, precisely because it is full of memories I stole from others: I stole them from Sandokan and Yanez racing their praus across the Malay seas.
quote.attribution: Umberto Eco, in Davide Ferrario's film Umberto Eco: La biblioteca del mondo (2022)

image.credit: Alberto della Valle (1851-1928), cover for the 1906 edition
image.alt: Cover of Salgari's Le Tigri di Mompracem, 1906 edition

stops.title: Emilio Salgari, Il Corsaro Nero
stops.caption: The Black Corsair, the Ligurian count turned Caribbean pirate, sworn to avenge his brothers. The row of Salgari in the living room holds the pirate cycle beside the Malaysian one.

source.label: Umberto Eco: La biblioteca del mondo (Davide Ferrario, 2022)

stops.title: Emilio Salgari, I misteri della jungla nera
stops.caption: Tremal-Naik, the hunter of the Black Jungle, against the Thugs of Kali: the first of the Indian novels and the book that introduced the villain Suyodhana. Eco defended exactly this kind of reading.

source.label: Umberto Eco: La biblioteca del mondo (Davide Ferrario, 2022)

quote.text: Quel tanto di vita che si conquista leggendo non discrimina tra grandi opere d'arte e letteratura di trattenimento: non fatevi ricattare da chi vi dice che bisogna leggere solo i libri importanti.
quote.translation: The extra life one gains by reading does not discriminate between great works of art and entertainment literature: don't let yourselves be blackmailed by those who tell you that one must read only important books.
quote.attribution: Umberto Eco, in Davide Ferrario's film Umberto Eco: La biblioteca del mondo (2022)

stops.title: Souvestre and Allain, Fantômas
stops.caption: The genius of crime in evening dress and a mask, thirty-two volumes written at speed between 1911 and 1913, adored by the surrealists and by every reader of the feuilleton. The first cover, with Fantômas striding over Paris, became the image of the whole series.

source.label: Umberto Eco: La biblioteca del mondo (Davide Ferrario, 2022)

image.alt: Cover of the first Fantômas (1911)

stops.title: Carlo Collodi, Pinocchio
stops.caption: The puppet who lies and grows a longer nose each time is a natural subject for a theorist of lying. Eco wrote the introduction to Geoffrey Brock's English Pinocchio in 2009, and once, with his students, rewrote the story with every word beginning with P.

source.label: Umberto Eco: La biblioteca del mondo (Davide Ferrario, 2022)

image.alt: Enrico Mazzanti's Pinocchio (1883)

stops.title: Vamba, Il giornalino di Gian Burrasca
stops.caption: The diary of Giannino Stoppani, the nine-year-old terror of his household, from 1912: the funniest book of Italian childhood, shelved in the corridor with the other boyhood classics.

source.label: Umberto Eco: La biblioteca del mondo (Davide Ferrario, 2022)

stops.title: Alexandre Dumas, Il conte di Montecristo
stops.caption: Eco's favourite badly written masterpiece. His essay in praise of Monte Cristo argues that the novel is gripping in spite of its prose, and admits that he once tried to translate it into better Italian and gave up.

source.label: Umberto Eco, 'Elogio del Montecristo' (1985)

quote.text: Montecristo è uno dei romanzi più appassionanti che mai siano stati scritti. In un colpo solo … riesce a inscatolare nello stesso romanzo tre situazioni archetipe capaci di torcere le viscere anche a un boia.
quote.translation: Monte Cristo is one of the most gripping novels ever written. In a single stroke it manages to pack into one novel three archetypal situations capable of wringing the guts even of an executioner.
quote.attribution: Umberto Eco, 'Elogio del Montecristo', in Sugli specchi e altri saggi (1985); text as reproduced on the blog Salvatore Lo Leggio (2012)

stops.title: Mémoires de M. d'Artagnan (Cologne, 1700)
stops.caption: The pseudo-memoirs by Courtilz de Sandras from which Dumas took d'Artagnan and the three musketeers. Eco kept the source in the rare room and the novels in the corridor. The first books he ever saw were his grandfather's unbound Dumas.

source.label: Biblioteca Nazionale Braidense, the record of Eco's copy

quote.text: So he had a lot of unbound books lying here and there around his apartment—old, beautifully illustrated editions of popular nineteenth-century novels by Gautier and Dumas. Those were the first books I ever saw.
quote.attribution: Umberto Eco, interviewed by Lila Azam Zanganeh, The Paris Review, 'The Art of Fiction No. 197' (2008)

stops.title: Alexandre Dumas, Ascanio
stops.caption: Dumas's novel of Benvenuto Cellini at the court of Francis I, from the years of the Musketeers. The shelf is a run of Dumas in nineteenth-century illustrated editions, the kind whose engravings Eco reused in The Prague Cemetery.

source.label: Biblioteca Nazionale Braidense, the record of Eco's copy

stops.title: Eugène Sue, Le Juif errant (1844 to 1845)
stops.caption: The Wandering Jew, Sue's serial about a Jesuit plot to seize an inheritance, illustrated by Louis Huard. Its picture of a Jesuit world conspiracy was one of the fictions that fed the Protocols, which is why it matters so much in The Prague Cemetery.

source.label: Biblioteca Nazionale Braidense, the record of Eco's copy

image.alt: Gavarni's illustration for Sue's Le Juif errant (1844 to 1845)

stops.title: Eugène Sue, Les mystères de Paris
stops.caption: The first great feuilleton, 1842 to 1843: Prince Rodolphe in disguise among the poor of Paris, the model of every serial that followed. Eco's Superuomo di massa returns to it and defends the pleasure such novels give.

source.label: Biblioteca Universitaria di Bologna, the record of Eco's copy

stops.title: Xavier de Montépin, Sa Majesté l'Argent
stops.caption: Montépin, the most prolific of the feuilletonists, with a novel on the majesty of money. The shelf of feuilletons is where Eco's Superuomo di massa was researched: the popular novelist as a manufacturer of consolation.

source.label: Biblioteca Nazionale Braidense, the record of Eco's copy

stops.title: Ponson du Terrail, le romancier à la plume infatigable
stops.caption: A life of the inventor of Rocambole, the hero whose adventures were so improbable that his name became a French word. Ponson wrote several serials at once and was said to have killed a character in one paper while he went on talking in another.

source.label: Biblioteca Universitaria di Bologna, the record of Eco's copy

stops.title: Carolina Invernizio, Matilde Serao, Liala
stops.caption: The women of the Italian popular novel, in a volume Eco co-wrote: Invernizio's kissed-and-abandoned heroines, Serao's Naples, Liala's aviators. Eco's interest in the consolatory novel did not stop at the border of good taste.

source.label: Biblioteca Universitaria di Bologna, the record of Eco's copy

stops.title: Peter Haining, The Sherlock Holmes Scrapbook
stops.caption: Fifty years of Holmesiana, as its subtitle has it. Eco read Conan Doyle as a semiotician: his essay on Holmes's method of inference, written with Thomas Sebeok's circle, treats the detective as a philosopher of signs, and William of Baskerville owes him his name.

source.label: Biblioteca Universitaria di Bologna, the record of Eco's copy

image.credit: Sidney Paget (1860-1908), 1903, for The Strand Magazine
image.alt: Holmes and Watson by Sidney Paget, The Strand Magazine (1903)

stops.title: Pierre Bayard, Il caso del mastino dei Baskerville
stops.caption: A French critic reopens The Hound of the Baskervilles and proves Holmes got the wrong murderer. Eco, who put a Baskerville into his own first novel, shelved it in the study.

source.label: Biblioteca Universitaria di Bologna, the record of Eco's copy

stops.title: Il caso Bond (1965)
stops.caption: The James Bond case: Eco's structural analysis of the Fleming plot, the nine moves every Bond novel makes, published in this collection he edited with Oreste del Buono. He was still bringing it up at dinner forty years later.

source.label: Umberto Eco, 'The Narrative Structure in Fleming' (1965)

stops.title: Ian Fleming, Casino Royale
stops.caption: The first Bond novel, 1953, and the first of the plots Eco took apart: M gives the mission, the villain appears, Bond is captured and tortured, Bond wins, Bond loses the woman.

source.label: Biblioteca Universitaria di Bologna, the record of Eco's copy

stops.title: Umberto Eco, Diario minimo (1963)
stops.caption: Eco's first book of parodies, which includes his praise of Franti, the bad boy of De Amicis's Cuore who laughs at the wrong moments. Eco took the side of the boy who smiled.

source.label: Umberto Eco, 'Elogio di Franti', in Diario minimo (1963)

stops.title: Eroi del racconto popolare
stops.caption: The heroes of popular storytelling, a study shelved among the heroes themselves at the point in the corridor where, Carlotta Eco says, she would begin any account of her father's library.

source.label: Umberto Eco: La biblioteca del mondo (Davide Ferrario, 2022)

quote.text: Se dovessi raccontare la biblioteca di mio padre inizierei da qua: sono i feuilleton, i romanzi d'appendice dell'Ottocento che lui ha letto da ragazzo e che in parte ha letto anche a noi.
quote.translation: If I had to tell the story of my father's library I would start from here: these are the feuilletons, the nineteenth-century serial novels that he read as a boy and partly read to us too.
quote.attribution: Carlotta Eco, in Davide Ferrario's film Umberto Eco: La biblioteca del mondo (2022)

walk.title: Eco's walk, 2015
walk.video_title: Umberto Eco, Sulla memoria. Una conversazione in tre parti, 2015. Parte 1. Regia di Davide Ferrario
walk.film_title: Umberto Eco: La biblioteca del mundo (2022) 1080p
walk.source: objects.README.md (experience folder): ten iconic moments with both clocks; route salotto > vestibolo > corridoio > study door > islands > desk > door I

waypoints.caption: Eco rises from the dark leather club armchair in front of the vitrines; the statue by the door ahead, the piano with its piles on the left.

quote.text: The library really is the symbol and the reality of a collective memory.
quote.text_it: La biblioteca è effettivamente simbolo e realtà di una memoria collettiva.
quote.source: Umberto Eco. La biblioteca del mondo (Davide Ferrario, 2022)
quote.speaker: Umberto Eco
quote.context: Interview in the study, 2015 (black and white), used over the opening long take

waypoints.caption: Out through the salotto door, past the white canvas with the word 'fine' and the column of small prints.
The vestibule: coats on both sides, the wall of framed prints, the white shelves B, C and D, the GOSH! pasta-flag picture straight ahead with the black mobile in front of it.
The turn into the long corridor through the doorway framed by bookcase D (esotericism, encyclopaedism, alchemy).

Bookcase A begins: twenty-five bays of fiction, the feuilletons at the centre, French literature along the line, Italian below, comics on the top and bottom shelves. The door of the Stanza degli antichi is on the print wall to the left.

quote.text: If I had to tell the story of my father's library I would start here: these are the feuilletons, the nineteenth-century serial novels he read as a boy and partly read to us too; and here are the beautiful engravings of the period, which he then used so much, above all in the novels, in The Prague Cemetery. … Here there is a marker: all of French literature stretches along this line, and here too; while below, for example, there is Italian literature, and if we go upwards instead we still stay within popular literature and arrive at the comics.
quote.text_it: Se dovessi raccontare la biblioteca di mio padre inizierei da qua: sono i feuilleton, i romanzi d'appendice dell'Ottocento che lui ha letto da ragazzo e che in parte ha letto anche a noi; e qui si trovano le immagini bellissime degli incisori del periodo, che lui poi ha utilizzato tantissimo, soprattutto nei romanzi, nel Cimitero di Praga. … Qui c'è un segnale: si estende un po' tutta la letteratura francese lungo questa linea, e anche qua; mentre qui sotto, ad esempio, c'è la letteratura italiana, e se andiamo invece verso l'alto rimaniamo sempre nell'ambito della letteratura popolare e arriviamo fino ai fumetti.
quote.source: Umberto Eco. La biblioteca del mondo (Davide Ferrario, 2022)
quote.speaker: Carlotta Eco

waypoints.caption: Halfway: the sliding ladder on its rail, the prints on the left wall. 'I have a hallway for literature that's 70 meters long. I walk through it several times a day, and I feel good when I do.'

quote.text: This working library is organised by sector, yes, but not alphabetically, rather by sub-sectors, where things then got moved around: almost only he knew where to find the books, because it was a living thing, not an archive, not a library codified in the classical sense.
quote.text_it: Questa biblioteca di lavoro è sì organizzata per settori, ma non alfabeticamente, piuttosto per sottosettori, dove poi alcune cose venivano spostate: lo sapeva quasi solo lui dove trovare i libri, perché era una cosa viva, non era un archivio, non era una biblioteca codificata nel senso classico.
quote.source: Umberto Eco. La biblioteca del mondo (Davide Ferrario, 2022)
quote.speaker: Stefano Eco

waypoints.caption: The corridor end: the French window with iron bars, the radiator below it, the speckled grey canvas.

quote.text: This library also has its own scent, a smell, and a sound too, I would say, because when you move through those corridors full of books everything is muffled: I feel very protected in there.
quote.text_it: Questa biblioteca ha anche un suo profumo, un odore, e anche un suono, direi, perché quando ti muovi in quei corridoi pieni di libri tutto è più attutito: io mi sento molto protetta lì in mezzo.
quote.source: Umberto Eco. La biblioteca del mondo (Davide Ferrario, 2022)
quote.speaker: Carlotta Eco
quote.context: Spoken over the corridor shots from 51:04; the speaker is on camera in the study from 51:15 as the sentence ends (the Italian 'protetta' is feminine).

waypoints.caption: Left turn past the folding step-ladder into the study, through the door framed by bookcase I (ancient and Christian philosophy).
The big study: the low island bookcases piled with books, the ceiling fans, the philosophy wall from the Presocratics to the moderns.
The aisle between the islands towards the windows.

quote.text: This is my father's study, in the house he and my mother chose thirty years ago so that his whole book collection could be kept: the 1,200 old books and the 30,000 modern ones.
quote.text_it: Qui siamo nello studio di mio padre, dentro la casa che lui e mia madre hanno scelto trent'anni fa per poter tenere tutta la collezione di libri di mio padre, cioè i 1.200 libri antichi e i 30.000 libri moderni.
quote.source: Umberto Eco. La biblioteca del mondo (Davide Ferrario, 2022)
quote.speaker: Stefano Eco

waypoints.caption: The L-shaped black desk with the computer under the windows, piles and papers on it, the dictionaries on the island behind.

quote.text: The flat is big precisely because otherwise the books would not fit: I was evicted from the previous one, with the civil engineers involved, because the bookcases seemed to be bringing the walls down.
quote.text_it: La casa è grande appunto perché i libri altrimenti non ci stanno: da quella precedente sono stato sfrattato, con un concorso del Genio civile, perché pareva che le librerie facessero crollare i muri.
quote.source: Umberto Eco. La biblioteca del mondo (Davide Ferrario, 2022)
quote.speaker: Umberto Eco

waypoints.caption: The door with the pinned notes (bookcase I): Eco takes down a red-spined book and leafs through it. The book is unidentified.
The final wide shot: Eco walks away down the study past the black round table and the sofa, the fans turning overhead.

quote.text: Vegetal memory, since books are unfortunately made of wood nowadays, and once of papyrus and so on: vegetal memory is the memory of books.
quote.text_it: La memoria vegetale, visto che i libri si fanno ormai col legno, ma una volta anche col papiro: la memoria vegetale è quella dei libri.
quote.source: Umberto Eco. La biblioteca del mondo (Davide Ferrario, 2022)
quote.speaker: Umberto Eco

route_notes.description: Eco in the cognac leather armchair, cigar-less, in front of the middle vitrine with the statue behind his shoulder; a white armchair beside him; sound boom with grey windscreen in the foreground; the camera is a static tripod shot at seated eye level from across the coffee table.
route_notes.note: Camera A: static, 1.1 m high, 3 m from the armchair, 35 mm lens.

route_notes.item: Eco rises and walks out of the salotto
route_notes.description: Start of the walk: Steadicam behind Eco at ~1.5 m; he crosses the salotto past the piano (left) and the statue (right) and goes through the door into the vestibule.
route_notes.note: Path point 1: salotto door, heading N; camera 1.5 m behind, 1.5 m high.

route_notes.description: Steadicam follows 1.5-2 m behind Eco (dark waistcoat, white shirt) down the corridor; the camera drifts right to graze the spines of case A; ceiling spots reflect; the balcony door grows at the end; 2015 part 1 t=309-327, film 62-80 s (b/w).
route_notes.note: Path points 3-4: straight 18 m walk, speed ~0.7 m/s; camera yaw slightly right.

route_notes.item: Eco turns left into the study past the step-ladder
route_notes.description: At the corridor end Eco turns left through the open door into the study; a folding stepladder and framed pictures at the door; the study islands and ceiling fans appear.
route_notes.note: Path point 5: 90-degree left turn 1.5 m before the balcony door.

route_notes.item: Eco walks between the islands to the desk
route_notes.description: He walks along an aisle between an island and the wall shelves toward the windows, passes a white cabinet and a framed picture, reaches the desk with the computer.
route_notes.note: Path points 6-7: 8 m along an island aisle to the desk by the windows.

route_notes.item: Eco takes a book down and leafs through it
route_notes.description: Beside the white door with pinned notes he reaches up to a shelf at ~1.8 m, pulls out a red-spined volume, opens it and reads for ~6 s, then puts it back and walks on (2015 part 1 t=351-359, film 104-112).
route_notes.note: Animation: stop at the door surround (case I), reach up, hold 6 s, replace; camera swings to a 3/4 front view.

route_notes.item: Eco walks away down the study (final wide shot)
route_notes.description: Final shot: the camera stays by the desk while Eco walks away between the desk and the wall shelves toward the far end of the study, under the ceiling fans, past piles on the desk and the black chairs; fade to black (2015 part 1 t=361-371; film 116-136 b/w).
route_notes.note: Camera fixed at the desk, 1.4 m high, wide lens; Eco walks 10 m away.

route_notes.item: Eco playing the recorder (archival, location uncertain)
route_notes.description: Archival clip of Eco playing a recorder at a rustic wooden music stand in front of shelves, next to a rough plank door: probably the Monte Cerignone house, not Milan.
route_notes.note: Do not place in Milan; reference only.

route_notes.item: Girl on roller skates (2022 epilogue walk)
route_notes.description: The film's epilogue re-runs the walk in reverse with a granddaughter on inline skates: rare-room dark corridor with prints -> long corridor toward the balcony door -> left into the study -> round table; useful as a second camera pass of the same route in colour.
route_notes.note: Alternative replay path in colour: film 4484-4512 s.

route_notes.description: Eco in the cognac armchair with the vitrines (shells and coral) soft-focus behind him; confirms the vitrine with natural objects stood behind the armchair in 2015.

The Braidense 'Studiolo Umberto Eco' (2022) rebuilt the rare room as a rectangle with the same cherry cabinets, oak table and exhibition cases; askanews clip shows it with visitors. Use only as a cross-check for cabinet proportions.

stops.title: Ficciones (incl. 'The Library of Babel', 'Death and the Compass')
stops.author: Borges, Jorge Luis
stops.why: The labyrinthine library as mirror of the world and the blind librarian Jorge of Burgos are Eco's homage to Borges; 'Death and the Compass' gives the false pattern of the murders.
stops.source: Eco, Postille a Il nome della rosa (1983) / Postscript to The Name of the Rose (1984); Eco, 'Borges and My Anxiety of Influence' in On Literature (2002); Lila Azam Zanganeh, 'Umberto Eco, The Art of Fiction No. 197', Paris Review 185 (2008) ('Usually I say Joyce and Borges')
stops.note: not found on these shelves; nothing by the author either: the stop shows the bookcase where its subject is shelved
stops.subject_rule: other literatures: Spanish, Portuguese, Latin American, Slavic (author)

stops.title: The Hound of the Baskervilles / the Sherlock Holmes stories
stops.author: Doyle, Arthur Conan
stops.why: William of Baskerville and Adso are modelled on Holmes and Watson; the opening deduction about the abbot's horse Brunellus is a Holmesian set piece.
stops.source: Eco, Postille a Il nome della rosa (1983) / Postscript to The Name of the Rose (1984); it.wikipedia 'Il nome della rosa' (sections on sources and characters), cross-read with Haft/White/White, The Key to The Name of the Rose (1987)
stops.note: not found on these shelves; nothing by the author either: the stop shows the bookcase where its subject is shelved

stops.title: Poetics (with the lost second book on comedy)
stops.author: Aristotle
stops.why: The murder weapon and the MacGuffin: the last copy of Aristotle's lost book on comedy, which Eco says he 'discovered' while writing the novel.

stops.title: Commentary on the Apocalypse (the Beatus tradition) and the Book of Revelation
stops.author: Beatus of Liébana
stops.why: The seven trumpets of the Apocalypse give the (false) pattern of the deaths; the abbey's illuminated Apocalypse manuscripts and the tympanum descriptions draw on Beatus imagery.
stops.source: it.wikipedia 'Il nome della rosa' (sections on sources and characters), cross-read with Haft/White/White, The Key to The Name of the Rose (1987) ('serie dei delitti ... ispirata alle sette trombe dell'Apocalisse')
stops.note: not found on these shelves; nothing by the author either: the stop shows the bookcase where its subject is shelved
stops.subject_rule: Aquinas, scholastic logic, medieval history and texts (title)

stops.title: Practica inquisitionis heretice pravitatis
stops.author: Gui, Bernard
stops.why: Bernard Gui appears as the inquisitor; his interrogation technique in the novel follows his real inquisitors' manual.
stops.source: it.wikipedia 'Il nome della rosa' (sections on sources and characters), cross-read with Haft/White/White, The Key to The Name of the Rose (1987); Haft/White/White, The Key to The Name of the Rose
stops.note: not found on these shelves; nothing by the author either: the stop shows the bookcase where its subject is shelved
stops.subject_rule: patristics, heresies, preaching, Greek religion, classical texts (title)

stops.title: Arbor vitae crucifixae Iesu
stops.author: Ubertino da Casale
stops.why: Ubertino is a character in the novel; Eco owned the 1485 Venice incunable and singled it out as one of the 'essentials' of his collection.

stops.title: Legenda aurea
stops.author: Jacobus de Voragine
stops.why: Source for the saints' lives and exempla the monks cite; standard reference behind the novel's hagiographic texture.
stops.source: Haft/White/White, The Key to The Name of the Rose (reference notes)
stops.note: not found on these shelves; nothing by the author either: the stop shows the room

stops.title: Opus maius
stops.author: Bacon, Roger
stops.why: William of Baskerville is made a disciple of Roger Bacon; Bacon's optics (spectacles), empiricism and prophecy of machines run through William's speeches.

stops.title: Summa logicae and the nominalist writings
stops.author: William of Ockham
stops.why: William of Baskerville's nominalism, his friendship with 'Ockham' and the closing 'nomina nuda tenemus' come from Ockham's philosophy.

stops.title: Coena Cypriani
stops.author: pseudo-Cyprian (anon., 5th-9th c.)
stops.why: The carnivalesque biblical banquet parody that Adso's great dream reproduces; the 'ioca monachorum' at the heart of the debate on laughter.
stops.source: Eco discusses the Coena in 'The Comic and the Rule' (Sette anni di desiderio) and it structures Adso's dream; see also academia.edu 'La Coena Cypriani fra pantagruelismi letterari'
stops.note: not found on these shelves; nothing by the author either: the stop shows the room

stops.title: Cronica
stops.author: Salimbene de Adam
stops.why: Chief chronicle source for Fra Dolcino, the Apostolics and the Franciscan disputes that Ubertino and William recount; the gossiping Franciscan voice of the 13th century.
stops.source: Haft/White/White, The Key to The Name of the Rose; Coletti, Naming the Rose (1988)
stops.note: not found on these shelves; nothing by the author either: the stop shows the room

stops.title: I promessi sposi (The Betrothed)
stops.author: Manzoni, Alessandro
stops.why: The 'found manuscript' frame ('Naturalmente, un manoscritto') and the narrator's ironic distance are borrowed from Manzoni; Eco also analyses its word frequencies and reader in Six Walks.

stops.title: Omnis mundi creatura / De planctu Naturae / Distinctiones
stops.author: Alain de Lille (Alanus de Insulis)
stops.why: The verse 'Omnis mundi creatura quasi liber et pictura' is quoted at the opening of the novel as William's view of the world as a book of signs; Eco owned Alanus's 1473 Distinctiones.

stops.title: Le Manuscrit de Dom Adson de Melk (Abbé Vallet, 1842) / Jean Mabillon, Vetera analecta
stops.author: Vallet, Abbé (fictional) / Mabillon, Jean
stops.why: The fictitious 19th-century edition and the real Benedictine scholar Mabillon form the chain of transmission in 'Naturalmente, un manoscritto'.
stops.source: Eco, Postille a Il nome della rosa (1983) / Postscript to The Name of the Rose (1984); it.wikipedia 'Il nome della rosa' (sections on sources and characters), cross-read with Haft/White/White, The Key to The Name of the Rose (1987)
stops.note: not found on these shelves; nothing by the author either: the stop shows the room

stops.title: Michael of Cesena and the poverty controversy (Franciscan sources; the Chronicle of Nicholas the Minorite)
stops.author: Michael of Cesena / Franciscan chronicles
stops.why: The papal legation and the debate on the poverty of Christ that frame the novel's plot; Michael of Cesena is a character.
stops.source: it.wikipedia 'Il nome della rosa' (sections on sources and characters), cross-read with Haft/White/White, The Key to The Name of the Rose (1987) ('generale dell'ordine dei frati minori')
stops.note: not found on these shelves; nothing by the author either: the stop shows the room

stops.title: Regula Sancti Benedicti
stops.author: Benedict of Nursia
stops.why: The canonical hours that divide each day of the novel and the monastic discipline of the abbey follow the Rule.
stops.source: inference from the novel; the hour-by-hour structure is noted in it.wikipedia 'Il nome della rosa' (sections on sources and characters), cross-read with Haft/White/White, The Key to The Name of the Rose (1987)
stops.note: not found on these shelves; nothing by the author either: the stop shows the room

stops.title: Physiologus and the medieval bestiaries
stops.author: anon. (Physiologus)
stops.why: The monsters of the tympanum, the marginalia of Adelmo and the abbey's animal lore come from the bestiary tradition; Eco's copy of Bartholomaeus Anglicus's encyclopaedia, the 1480 Lyon incunable, carries the same lore.
stops.source: Haft/White/White, Key; inference from the novel
stops.note: not found on these shelves; nothing by the author either: the stop shows the bookcase where its subject is shelved

stops.title: Etymologiae
stops.author: Isidore of Seville
stops.why: The encyclopaedic source Adso and William cite for names, monsters and the sciences; Eco owned the 1473 Strasbourg incunable.

stops.title: De contemptu mundi
stops.author: Bernard of Cluny (Morlaix)
stops.why: The last line of the novel, 'Stat rosa pristina nomine, nomina nuda tenemus', is taken from this poem; Eco explains it in the Postscript.
stops.source: Eco, Postille a Il nome della rosa (1983) / Postscript to The Name of the Rose (1984); it.wikipedia 'Il nome della rosa' (sections on sources and characters), cross-read with Haft/White/White, The Key to The Name of the Rose (1987)
stops.note: not found on these shelves; nothing by the author either: the stop shows the room

stops.title: Là-bas / La Cathédrale
stops.author: Huysmans, Joris-Karl
stops.why: Huysmans's decadent-Catholic novels of cathedrals, satanism and monastic longing lie behind the abbey atmosphere; Là-bas is later quoted 'rather literally' for the Black Mass in The Prague Cemetery.

stops.title: Ulysses
stops.author: Joyce, James
stops.why: The division of the novel into the hours of a day (canonical hours) is a borrowing from Ulysses; Joyce was the subject of Eco's early study Le poetiche di Joyce.

stops.title: Divina Commedia
stops.author: Dante Alighieri
stops.why: Quoted in the novel ('Caddi come corpo morto cade'); Eco's Braidense holds Landino's 1491 commented Dante and the 'hermetic' Dante readings (Rossetti, Aroux, Valli) he used as examples of overinterpretation.

stops.title: Pseudodoxia Epidemica / Religio Medici
stops.author: Browne, Sir Thomas
stops.why: Often cited as an ancestor of Eco's taste for catalogues of 'vulgar errors' and of William's sceptical erudition; not a documented direct source.
stops.source: inference from the novel (no documentation of a direct link found)
stops.note: not found on these shelves; nothing by the author either: the stop shows the bookcase where its subject is shelved

stops.title: Tractatus logico-philosophicus
stops.author: Wittgenstein, Ludwig
stops.why: William's image, on the novel's last night, of the ladder that must be thrown away after climbing is Wittgenstein's (Tractatus 6.54), given in medieval German as a fourteenth-century saying.

stops.title: Ars magna lucis et umbrae
stops.author: Kircher, Athanasius
stops.why: Kircher's optics and magic lantern are among the chapter-title sources of The Island of the Day Before and the Kircherian universe of Foucault's Pendulum; Eco owned both editions and called himself a 'Kircher fan'.

stops.title: Oedipus Aegyptiacus
stops.author: Kircher, Athanasius
stops.why: Kircher's monumental mis-reading of the hieroglyphs is the model of 'hermetic drift' that Eco taught in 1992 and mocks in the Plan; central case in The Search for the Perfect Language.

stops.title: Mundus subterraneus
stops.author: Kircher, Athanasius
stops.why: Kircher's underground world of fires and currents feeds the novel's telluric currents and the 'Umbilicus Mundi'; also a chapter title in The Island of the Day Before.

stops.title: Turris Babel
stops.author: Kircher, Athanasius
stops.why: Kircher's Babel (with the plate of the tower's impossible height) is one of the Fondazione's ten highlighted rare books and Eco's favourite Kircher anecdote.

stops.title: China monumentis illustrata
stops.author: Kircher, Athanasius
stops.why: 'The first to publish a sort of encyclopaedia about China', as Jean-Claude Carrière put it to Eco; one of the ten rare books the Fondazione shows from the Stanza degli antichi.

stops.title: Utriusque cosmi maioris scilicet et minoris metaphysica, physica atque technica historia
stops.author: Fludd, Robert
stops.why: Fludd's macrocosm/microcosm engravings are the visual grammar of the Plan; Eco: 'I also possess the works of Robert Fludd'; the Fondazione highlights his 1619 volume.

stops.title: Ars magna / Ars brevis
stops.author: Llull, Ramon
stops.why: Lull's combinatorial wheels are the model for Abulafia the computer and the permutations of the Plan; long chapter in The Search for the Perfect Language.

stops.title: Steganographia
stops.author: Trithemius, Johannes
stops.why: Trithemius's angel-cipher book is the archetype of the secret message in the Plan; discussed in The Search for the Perfect Language and Serendipities; Eco owned five editions, printed between 1606 and 1721.

stops.title: Polygraphiae libri sex
stops.author: Trithemius, Johannes
stops.why: The first printed book on cryptography; Eco owned the 1518 editio princeps and the 1561 French translation.

stops.title: De occulta philosophia libri tres
stops.author: Agrippa von Nettesheim, Heinrich Cornelius
stops.why: The Renaissance summa of magic quoted by the Diabolicals; Eco owned the 1533 first complete edition.

stops.title: Monas hieroglyphica
stops.author: Dee, John
stops.why: Dee's hieroglyphic monad and his angel conversations are staged in the Plan's Elizabethan chapter; Eco owned the 1564 first edition and the 1659 True & Faithful Relation.

stops.title: De umbris idearum
stops.author: Bruno, Giordano
stops.why: Bruno's memory wheels and hermetic cosmology, read through Yates, are among the materials of the Plan; Eco owned the 1582 Paris first edition.

stops.title: Opera omnia (Paracelsus)
stops.author: Paracelsus (Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim)
stops.why: Paracelsian alchemy pervades the Diabolicals' talk; Eco owned the 1658 Opera and told Carrière of 'an old Paracelsus so heavily annotated ... every page looks like a piece of lace'.

stops.title: Fama Fraternitatis / Confessio Fraternitatis (Rosicrucian manifestos)
stops.author: anon. (Andreae circle)
stops.why: The Rosicrucian manifestos are the historical 'hoax that became true' at the heart of the Plan; Eco owned the 1615 Fama and a run of the 1615-1625 pamphlet war, and told Carrière how he had Gutman's Offenbarung, the book said to have inspired the manifestos, bought for him at a Munich auction.

stops.title: Atalanta fugiens
stops.author: Maier, Michael
stops.why: The alchemical emblem book with fugues; a coloured copy is one of the Fondazione's ten highlighted rare books and among the Studiolo's treasures.

stops.title: Geheime Figuren der Rosenkreuzer
stops.author: anon.
stops.why: The coloured Altona Rosicrucian plates; one of the ten highlighted rare books of the Stanza degli antichi.

stops.title: Les Prophéties (Centuries)
stops.author: Nostradamus
stops.why: Quoted by the Diabolicals as proof of the Plan; no Nostradamus edition in the exports.

stops.title: Dogme et rituel de la haute magie
stops.author: Lévi, Eliphas (Alphonse-Louis Constant)
stops.why: Lévi's 19th-century occult revival (Baphomet, tarot, Kabbalah) is the immediate idiom of Agliè and the Diabolicals.

stops.title: Corpus Hermeticum (Pimander), Ficino's translation
stops.author: Hermes Trismegistus / Ficino, Marsilio
stops.why: The ur-text of hermeticism, dated by Isaac Casaubon (the narrator's namesake) to the early centuries CE rather than to remote antiquity; Eco lists Ficino's Corpus Hermeticum among the 'essentials' of his incunabula.

stops.title: Picatrix
stops.author: pseudo-Majriti
stops.why: The Arabic-Latin grimoire of talismanic magic cited in the Plan's genealogy of occultism.

stops.title: Les Mystères de la cathédrale de Chartres / Les Mystères templiers
stops.author: Charpentier, Louis
stops.why: Charpentier's Templar-and-Gothic numerology is the kind of 'proof' Colonel Ardenti recites; a source of the Plan's Templar layer.

stops.title: The Holy Blood and the Holy Grail
stops.author: Baigent, Michael; Leigh, Richard; Lincoln, Henry
stops.why: The Plan parodies this bestseller's Priory-of-Sion 'history'; Eco's target for what he called paranoid interpretation.
stops.source: en.wikipedia 'Foucault's Pendulum' (novel read as parody of Holy Blood, Holy Grail); Cambridge, Umberto Eco and the Open Text ch. 6
stops.note: not found on these shelves; the nearest book by the same author is 'Il Santo Graal'

stops.title: Giordano Bruno and the Hermetic Tradition
stops.author: Yates, Frances A.
stops.why: Yates's reconstruction of Renaissance hermeticism is the scholarly scaffolding of the Plan and of Eco's 'hermetic drift' in The Limits of Interpretation.

stops.title: The Art of Memory
stops.author: Yates, Frances A.
stops.why: Behind the memory-theatre imagery of the Plan and Eco's ars memoriae collection (Romberch, Rosselli, Camillo, Bruno).

stops.title: The Rosicrucian Enlightenment
stops.author: Yates, Frances A.
stops.why: Yates's account of the manifestos and their 'furore' is the historical backbone of the Rosicrucian chapters of the Plan.
stops.source: inference from the novel; Yates is cited throughout Eco's 1990-92 essays on interpretation
stops.note: not found on these shelves; the nearest book by the same author is 'L'arte della memoria'

stops.title: Les Templiers sont parmi nous
stops.author: Sède, Gérard de
stops.why: De Sède's Gisors treasure books are the French 'Templar revival' that Ardenti and the Diabolicals reproduce.

stops.title: Secret Societies and Subversive Movements
stops.author: Webster, Nesta H.
stops.why: Webster's grand conspiracy history (Templars-Illuminati-Jews) has the shape of the Plan, and Eco discusses her in his lecture on fictional protocols; Eco owned the 1924 first edition.

stops.title: The Protocols of the Elders of Zion
stops.author: anonymous (compiled from Joly and Goedsche; the compilers are disputed)
stops.why: The paradigm forgery: discussed in Foucault's Pendulum, Six Walks ('Fictional Protocols'), Inventing the Enemy, and made the object of The Prague Cemetery.

stops.title: Horologium oscillatorium
stops.author: Huygens, Christiaan
stops.why: The founding treatise on pendulum motion sits in Eco's earliest-books section, a physical footnote to the novel's title object.

stops.title: Kabbala denudata
stops.author: Knorr von Rosenroth, Christian
stops.why: The Latin Kabbalah anthology through which Diotallevi's sefirot (the novel's ten sections) reached Christian Europe.

stops.title: Sefer Yetzirah
stops.author: anon.
stops.why: The Book of Creation, whose letter-combinatorics (and Abulafia's) underlie the naming of Belbo's computer and the Plan's permutations.

notable_tours.title: The Island of the Day Before (1994)

stops.title: Il cannocchiale aristotelico
stops.author: Tesauro, Emanuele
stops.why: Father Emanuele and his 'Aristotelian machine' of metaphors are Tesauro; a chapter of the novel carries the book's title.

stops.title: Technica curiosa / Magia universalis / Schola steganographica
stops.author: Schott, Gaspar
stops.why: Father Caspar Wanderdrossel is built from Gaspar Schott and Kircher; 'Technica curiosa' is a chapter title; Eco: 'I also have the works of ... Gaspar Schott'.

stops.title: Apiaria universae philosophiae mathematicae
stops.author: Bettini, Mario
stops.why: Jesuit mathematical curiosities of the kind Father Caspar deploys; not found in the exports.
stops.source: inference from the novel
stops.note: not found on these shelves; nothing by the author either: the stop shows the bookcase where its subject is shelved

stops.title: A Late Discourse ... Touching the Cure of Wounds by the Powder of Sympathy
stops.author: Digby, Sir Kenelm
stops.why: The 'Powder of Sympathy' (weapon salve) is the novel's longitude scheme and a chapter title. Eco owned the 1658 and 1681 French editions.

stops.title: Dialogo sopra i due massimi sistemi del mondo
stops.author: Galilei, Galileo
stops.why: The Jupiter-moons method of longitude and the chapter 'Dialoghi dei massimi sistemi'; Eco pointedly did not collect Galileo ('I have Ptolemy, who was wrong ... but not Galileo, who was right').
stops.source: Eco & Carrière, This Is Not the End of the Book (2011), ch. 'Every book published today is a post-incunabulum'; inference from the novel
stops.note: not found on these shelves; the nearest book by the same author is 'Against the Donning of the Gown ; Enigma'
stops.nearest_title: Against the Donning of the Gown ; Enigma

stops.title: L'Autre Monde: Les États et Empires de la Lune
stops.author: Cyrano de Bergerac, Savinien
stops.why: Saint-Savin is Cyrano; the lunar voyages and libertine cosmology of the novel come from him.
stops.note: Eco's copy of the author's collected works, which contain the work

stops.title: The Anatomy of Melancholy
stops.author: Burton, Robert
stops.why: Roberto's love-melancholy draws on the seventeenth-century literature of melancholy of which Burton's Anatomy is the great compendium; the chapter devoted to it is 'Della malattia d'amore o melanconia erotica'.

stops.title: Hydrographie / Geographiae et hydrographiae reformatae libri XII
stops.author: Fournier, Georges / Riccioli, Giovanni Battista
stops.why: Baroque navigation and longitude treatises behind the Daphne's voyage; Eco owned Riccioli's Geographia et hydrographia reformata (1672) and Medina's Arte del navigare.

stops.title: The Discovery of a World in the Moone / Essay towards a Real Character
stops.author: Wilkins, John
stops.why: Wilkins's plurality of worlds and his universal language are baroque themes of the novel and a central chapter of The Search for the Perfect Language; Eco owned the 1668 Essay and the 1708 Works.

stops.title: Longitudinum terrestrium necnon coelestium nova et hactenus optata scientia
stops.author: Morin, Jean-Baptiste
stops.why: A 17th-century longitude proposal of exactly the kind the novel satirises (Morin claimed Richelieu's prize); Eco owned it, together with d'Arcons's 'Secret du flux et reflux ... et des longitudes' (1655).

stops.title: De sensu rerum et magia
stops.author: Campanella, Tommaso
stops.why: The 'sense of things' (stones that feel) is the panpsychist doctrine debated on the Daphne, and the novel gives a whole chapter to how stones might think.

stops.title: Itinerarium exstaticum
stops.author: Kircher, Athanasius
stops.why: Kircher's cosmic voyage supplies the chapter 'Itinerarium extaticum coeleste' and Father Caspar's astronomy.

stops.title: Delle navigationi et viaggi
stops.author: Ramusio, Giovanni Battista
stops.why: The great collection of voyages, kept among his most precious books; part of the 'corner of travel literature' the family identified as sources of L'isola del giorno prima.

stops.title: Isolario
stops.author: Bordone, Benedetto
stops.why: The Renaissance book of all the islands of the world, an emblem of the novel's island obsession; shelved among Eco's earliest books.

stops.title: Chronica sive Historia de duabus civitatibus
stops.author: Otto of Freising
stops.why: Baudolino writes over a palimpsest of Otto's Chronica and forges Otto's texts; Otto is the first to mention Prester John. Eco owned the 1515 Strasbourg edition.
stops.source: Bologna libraries 'Ottone di Frisinga e Rahewino' (Baudolino album); en.wikipedia 'Baudolino'
stops.note: not found on these shelves; the nearest book by the same author is 'Ottonis Phrisingensis episcopi, ... Rerum ab origine mundi ad ipsius vsque tempo'
stops.nearest_title: Ottonis Phrisingensis episcopi, ... Rerum ab origine mundi ad ipsius vsque tempora gestarum, libri octo. Eiusdem De gestis Friderici primi Aenobarbi C

stops.title: The Letter of Prester John
stops.author: anon. (12th-c. forgery)
stops.why: 'One of the most delightful falsities in all western history': Baudolino and friends compose the letter; the seminal idea of the novel.
stops.source: Eco quoted in Biblioteche Bologna 'Il Prete Gianni' (Baudolino album); en.wikipedia 'Baudolino'
stops.note: not found on these shelves; nothing by the author either: the stop shows the bookcase where its subject is shelved

stops.title: The Travels of Sir John Mandeville
stops.author: Mandeville, John
stops.why: The monsters of the East (skiapods, blemmyae, panotii) that Baudolino meets are lifted from Mandeville.
stops.source: en.wikipedia 'Baudolino' ('some derived from The Travels of Sir John Mandeville')
stops.note: not found on these shelves; the nearest book by the same author is 'Viaggi, ovvero Trattato delle cose piu meravigliose e piu notabili che si trovan'
stops.nearest_title: Viaggi, ovvero Trattato delle cose piu meravigliose e piu notabili che si trovano al mondo

stops.title: The Alexander Romance
stops.author: pseudo-Callisthenes
stops.why: The eastern marvels and the enclosed peoples of Gog and Magog in Baudolino's journey come from the Alexander tradition.
stops.source: inference from the novel
stops.note: not found on these shelves; nothing by the author either: the stop shows the room

stops.title: Historia (Chronike diegesis)
stops.author: Choniates, Niketas
stops.why: Niketas is the listener to whom Baudolino tells his life during the 1204 sack of Constantinople; his history is the novel's Byzantine source. Eco owned Wolf's Greek-and-Latin edition of 1557 and the Italian translation of 1562.

stops.title: Joseph d'Arimathie / the Grail romances (Robert de Boron; Wolfram's Parzival and 'Kyot')
stops.author: Robert de Boron; Wolfram von Eschenbach
stops.why: Baudolino's Gradal (a wooden bowl) parodies the Grail legend; Robert de Boron and the invented source 'Kyot' appear as characters.
stops.source: en.wikipedia 'Baudolino' (Robert de Boron among historical characters; Kyot)
stops.note: not found on these shelves; nothing by the author either: the stop shows the bookcase where its subject is shelved
stops.subject_rule: Aquinas, scholastic logic, medieval history and texts (title)

stops.title: De proprietatibus rerum
stops.author: Bartholomaeus Anglicus
stops.why: The 13th-century encyclopaedia of natural marvels behind the monsters of Baudolino and the Rose; Eco owned the 1480 incunable.

stops.title: Dialogue aux enfers entre Machiavel et Montesquieu
stops.author: Joly, Maurice
stops.why: The anti-Bonapartist satire plagiarised by the forgers of the Protocols; Eco 'correctly identifies' it as the source and Simonini steals from it.

stops.title: Biarritz (chapter 'In the Jewish Cemetery in Prague')
stops.author: Goedsche, Hermann ('Sir John Retcliffe')
stops.why: The Prague-cemetery scene that gives the novel its title; Simonini's forged report is its 'source'. Eco owned the 1924 reprint.

stops.title: Le Juif errant
stops.author: Sue, Eugène
stops.why: Simonini reads Sue's Jesuit-conspiracy novel; its villain Father Rodin returns in Les Mystères du peuple with the letter that Simonini recycles into the Prague cemetery speech; Eco owned the 1846 Brussels edition, named among the Studiolo highlights.

stops.title: Les Mystères du peuple
stops.author: Sue, Eugène
stops.why: The second Sue source, the Jesuit plan for world domination set out in Father Rodin's letter, from which Simonini builds the forgery. Les Mystères du peuple itself is not among the catalogued volumes; Eco's two-volume Oeuvres illustrées of 1850 (Latréaumont, Mathilde and five other works) is in the Braidense.
stops.note: Eco's copy of the author's collected works, which contain the work

stops.title: Joseph Balsamo (Mémoires d'un médecin)
stops.author: Dumas, Alexandre
stops.why: Dumas's Masonic-conspiracy opening (Cagliostro on the Donnersberg) is, via Goedsche, a narrative source of the Protocols and of Simonini's forgery.
stops.source: Massimo Introvigne, 'C'è complotto e complotto. Il cimitero di Praga di Umberto Eco' (CESNUR, 2010); Letture.org summary ('Dumas's Giuseppe Balsamo through Goedsche')
stops.note: not found on these shelves; the nearest book by the same author is 'Ascanio, vol. 1'

stops.title: Les Frères Trois-Points / Les Mystères de la Franc-Maçonnerie / Le Diable au XIXe siècle
stops.author: Taxil, Léo (Gabriel Jogand-Pagès) with 'Dr Bataille'
stops.why: Taxil's anti-Masonic hoax and the Diana Vaughan affair fill the last third of the novel; Eco collected Taxil: six of his works are in the Braidense fund.

stops.title: Mémoires d'une ex-palladiste / Le 33e Crispi
stops.author: Vaughan, Diana (Taxil hoax)
stops.why: The invented convert whose 'memoirs' Simonini helps fabricate; Eco owned modern reprints of the Vaughan pamphlets.

stops.title: Le Juif, le judaïsme et la judaïsation des peuples chrétiens
stops.author: Gougenot des Mousseaux, Roger
stops.why: Simonini meets Gougenot; his 1869 book is the anti-Semitic 'world conquest' thesis the novel tracks into Drumont. Eco owned Gougenot's two magic books.
stops.source: Letture.org / Nazione Indiana summaries of the novel's sources; Braidense records
stops.note: not found on these shelves; the nearest book by the same author is 'La magie au dix-neuviéme siécle'

stops.title: La France juive
stops.author: Drumont, Édouard
stops.why: Drumont is a character; his bestseller (partly recycled from Gougenot) is the Parisian anti-Semitic milieu of the novel. Eco's copy is the one-volume illustrated Blériot edition, undated; its preface is dated December 1885.

stops.title: Mémoires pour servir à l'histoire du jacobinisme
stops.author: Barruel, Augustin
stops.why: The founding text of the Masonic-conspiracy reading of the Revolution, opening the novel's genealogy (Simonini's grandfather writes to Barruel). Eco owned the 4-volume 1799 edition.

stops.title: L'uomo delinquente
stops.author: Lombroso, Cesare
stops.why: Simonini's physiognomic racism speaks Lombroso's language; the very first shelfmark of Eco's library, ECO.01.0001, is L'uomo delinquente, and this 1924 Bocca edition stands at ECO.01.0007 among Mantegazza and the physiognomists.

stops.title: Studies on Hysteria / Charcot's lessons
stops.author: Freud, Sigmund and Breuer, Josef; Charcot, Jean-Martin
stops.why: The young 'Dr Froïde' and Charcot's Salpêtrière appear in the novel; Simonini's split personality is written as a case of hysteria/dissociation.
stops.note: Eco's copy of the author's collected works, which contain the work

stops.title: Les Juifs, rois de l'époque
stops.author: Toussenel, Alphonse
stops.why: Early socialist anti-Semitic tract of the milieu Eco reconstructs; owned in the 1847 edition.

stops.title: Indagine sul satanismo
stops.author: Introvigne, Massimo
stops.why: Introvigne says Eco followed his 1994 study 'ampiamente' for the Taxil and Boullan material.
stops.source: Massimo Introvigne, 'C'è complotto e complotto. Il cimitero di Praga di Umberto Eco' (CESNUR, 2010) ('seguendo ampiamente il mio Indagine sul satanismo del 1994')

stops.title: Flash Gordon

stops.why: Eco's 'Elogio del Montecristo' (in Sugli specchi / On Literature) defends the badly-written masterpiece; part of his popular-fiction canon.
stops.source: Eco, 'In Praise of The Count of Monte Cristo' in On Literature (2002)
stops.note: not found on these shelves; the nearest book by the same author is 'Ascanio, vol. 1'

stops.title: She
stops.author: Haggard, H. Rider
stops.why: The Loana comic is a rip-off of She; the 'mysterious flame' of immortality is Haggard's.
stops.source: it.wikipedia Queen Loana
stops.note: not found on these shelves; nothing by the author either: the stop shows the room

stops.title: Shakespeare, First Folio (1623)
stops.author: Shakespeare, William
stops.why: The book whose discovery in the grandfather's library gives Yambo his second stroke; Eco calls the Folio 'the holy of holies' of collecting.
stops.source: it.wikipedia Queen Loana; Eco & Carrière, This Is Not the End of the Book (2011), ch. 'Every book published today is a post-incunabulum' (the Folio as 'holy of holies')
stops.note: not found on these shelves; nothing by the author either: the stop shows the bookcase where its subject is shelved

stops.title: Martin Eden
stops.author: London, Jack
stops.why: Named in the novel as one of Yambo's formative books.
stops.source: it.wikipedia Queen Loana
stops.note: not found on these shelves; nothing by the author either: the stop shows the room

stops.title: Cyrano de Bergerac
stops.author: Rostand, Edmond
stops.why: Rostand's Cyrano is one of the texts through which Yambo recovers his first love; Eco owned an 1898 printing in the rare room.

stops.title: Braccio di Ferro (Popeye)
stops.author: Segar, Elzie Crisler
stops.why: One of the childhood comics; the Bologna catalogue has Eco's 1965 Italian reprint.

stops.title: Il grande complotto (Mussolini's death, Gladio, P2 literature)
stops.author: various
stops.why: Braggadocio's paranoid history in Numero Zero is built from the 1990s Italian literature on Mussolini's 'double', Gladio and P2; no single documented book source.

stops.title: Hypnerotomachia Poliphili
stops.author: Colonna, Francesco
stops.why: 'Possibly the most beautiful book in the world' and the pride of the collection; Eco jokes that his block by the Castello has the world's highest concentration of Hypnerotomachiae.

stops.title: Liber chronicarum (Nuremberg Chronicle)
stops.author: Schedel, Hartmann
stops.why: Named by Eco among the 'essentials' of his incunabula; he tells the story of the New York dealer who broke copies up to sell pages.

stops.title: De civitate Dei
stops.author: Augustine of Hippo
stops.why: The 1470 Rome edition is the oldest book in the collection and was named in the Studiolo press as one of its treasures.

stops.title: Malleus maleficarum
stops.author: Kramer, Heinrich (Institoris)
stops.why: Eco's incunable of the witch-hunting manual, bound by a 'Horned Moses' Jewish binder for Cistercian libraries: his favourite provenance story.

stops.title: Almagest / Tetrabiblos / Geographia
stops.author: Ptolemy, Claudius
stops.why: The emblem of the collection's principle: 'I have Ptolemy, who was wrong about the movement of the Earth, but not Galileo, who was right'.

stops.title: The Voynich manuscript (as 'The Cipher of Roger Bacon')
stops.author: Newbold, William Romaine / anon.
stops.why: Eco's interest in the undeciphered manuscript is represented by Newbold's 1928 'decipherment' attributing it to Roger Bacon; no facsimile found in the exports.

stops.title: Les Fous littéraires
stops.author: Blavier, André / Brunet, Gustave ('Philomneste junior')
stops.why: The bibliographies of 'literary madmen' that map the 'lunatica' side of the Bibliotheca semiologica; the 19th-century French cranks of section ECO.02, the books kept on the desk and around the rare-book room, keep them company.

stops.title: Trattato dei tre impostori (De tribus impostoribus)
stops.author: anon.
stops.why: The legendary non-existent blasphemous book, a favourite case in Eco's essays on imaginary books and forgeries.

stops.title: Museum Wormianum
stops.author: Worm, Ole
stops.why: The Wunderkammer catalogue with the famous frontispiece; among the ten highlighted rare books and the Studiolo treasures (Eco kept real mirabilia beside his books).

stops.title: Thesaurus animalium / Thesaurus anatomicus
stops.author: Ruysch, Frederik
stops.why: Ruysch's anatomical dioramas: one of the Fondazione's ten highlighted rare books (the 1744 Opera set).

stops.title: Le relationi universali
stops.author: Botero, Giovanni
stops.why: Botero's world description with its part on 'mostri & usanze' of the Indies; one of the ten highlighted rare books.

stops.title: Emblemata
stops.author: Schoonhoven, Florentius
stops.why: One of the ten highlighted rare books; represents Eco's emblem-book shelf (Alciato, Valeriano, Ripa, Camerarii, Vaenius).

stops.title: Catalogo degli ordini religiosi / equestri
stops.author: Bonanni, Filippo
stops.why: One of the ten highlighted rare books (captioned by the Fondazione).

stops.title: Histoires prodigieuses
stops.author: Boaistuau, Pierre
stops.why: The first French book of monsters and prodigies; Eco's copy is the 1560 Paris first edition, printed for Longis and Le Mangnier.

stops.title: Monstrorum historia / De animalibus insectis
stops.author: Aldrovandi, Ulisse
stops.why: Eco showed his family 'animals, monsters and creatures from books by Aldrovandi and Kircher'; the Braidense holds his Aldrovandi volumes.

stops.title: De harmonia mundi totius cantica tria
stops.author: Zorzi (Giorgio), Francesco
stops.why: Named by the Braidense curators among the collection's treasures; Zorzi's kabbalistic harmony of the cosmos is the kind of numerology the Plan of Foucault's Pendulum runs on.

stops.title: Compendio della vita e delle gesta di Giuseppe Balsamo denominato il conte Cagliostro
stops.author: anon. (Roman Inquisition)
stops.why: Cagliostro is one of Eco's exemplary impostors (Prague Cemetery, Foucault's Pendulum); the 1791 Inquisition life is in the rare room.

stops.title: Arcana coelestia / The Apocalypse explained
stops.author: Swedenborg, Emanuel
stops.why: Swedenborg's visionary exegesis, collected in the 19th-century English sets, belongs to the 'pneumatica' side of the Bibliotheca.

stops.title: La Décadence latine / Salon de la Rose-Croix
stops.author: Péladan, Joséphin (Sâr)
stops.why: The fin-de-siècle Rosicrucian occultists (Péladan, Guaita, Papus) are the milieu of the Diabolicals and of Simonini's Paris; a whole run sits in ECO.02.

notable_tours.title: Essays: Kircher, Lull and the occult

stops.title: Magia naturalis / De furtivis literarum notis
stops.author: Della Porta, Giovanni Battista
stops.why: Twenty books of natural magic, from magnets and lenses to invisible writing, by the Neapolitan whose cipher treatise of 1563, De furtivis literarum notis, Eco names among the polygraphies in The Search for the Perfect Language.

stops.title: De subtilitate / Somniorum synesiorum / Metoposcopia
stops.author: Cardano, Girolamo
stops.why: Cardano's dream-interpretation and face-reading are staples of the 'mistaken sciences'; five of his works stand on Eco's shelves, beside Scaliger's Exercitationes against his De subtilitate.

stops.title: Ars magna sciendi
stops.author: Kircher, Athanasius
stops.why: Kircher's Lullian combinatorial 'great art' links the Lull and Kircher shelves; a key text in The Search for the Perfect Language.

stops.title: Musurgia universalis
stops.author: Kircher, Athanasius
stops.why: Kircher on music and sound machines; part of the near-complete Kircher run (all but Ars magnesia).

stops.title: Magnes sive De arte magnetica
stops.author: Kircher, Athanasius
stops.why: Kircher's magnetism (the 'Ars magnesia' Eco could never find is its precursor); Digby's sympathy powder in The Island belongs to the same world.

stops.title: Idea del theatro
stops.author: Camillo, Giulio
stops.why: Camillo's memory theatre, the centrepiece of Yates's Art of Memory and of Eco's ars memoriae shelf.

stops.title: Congestorium artificiosae memoriae
stops.author: Romberch, Johannes
stops.why: The illustrated Dominican memory treatise; one of some thirty ars memoriae books (Rosselli, Chappuys and Velázquez de Azevedo among them) shelved together in ECO.01.07xx.

stops.title: De republica / De universitate (Postel)
stops.author: Postel, Guillaume
stops.why: Postel's Hebrew-as-original-language and universal restitution are a chapter of The Search for the Perfect Language; nine Braidense records of his works.

stops.title: Amphitheatrum sapientiae aeternae
stops.author: Khunrath, Heinrich
stops.why: The most famous illustrated alchemical-kabbalistic book; 1609 edition in Eco's earliest-books section.

stops.title: Iconologia
stops.author: Ripa, Cesare
stops.why: The allegorical dictionary of Baroque imagery; Eco's copy is the 1603 Rome edition, the first with woodcuts.

stops.title: Hieroglyphica
stops.author: Horapollo / Valeriano, Pierio
stops.why: The Renaissance hieroglyph tradition (Horapollo 1519/1542/1551, Valeriano 1556/1621) that Kircher inherits; the pre-history of Eco's hieroglyph course.

stops.title: Theatrum orbis terrarum
stops.author: Ortelius, Abraham
stops.why: The first modern atlas, 1575 edition, in the earliest-books section; Eco's Book of Legendary Lands draws on such maps.

stops.title: Atlantis: the Antediluvian World
stops.author: Donnelly, Ignatius
stops.why: The founding text of modern Atlantis lore, treated in The Book of Legendary Lands; 1910 edition owned.

stops.title: Collected Papers
stops.author: Peirce, Charles Sanders
stops.why: 'Undoubtedly the greatest American philosopher and the father of semiotics'; the foundation of Eco's theory of interpretation (Limits of Interpretation).

stops.title: Essais de linguistique générale
stops.author: Jakobson, Roman
stops.why: Jakobson's functions of language are a pillar of A Theory of Semiotics; not yet in the exports.

stops.title: Éléments de sémiologie / L'analyse structurale du récit
stops.author: Barthes, Roland
stops.why: Barthes's structural semiology (Communications 8, 1966) is the milieu of Eco's La struttura assente (1968).

stops.title: Estetica: teoria della formatività
stops.author: Pareyson, Luigi
stops.why: Eco's Turin teacher; the theory of 'formatività' underlies Opera aperta (1962).

stops.title: Cours de linguistique générale
stops.author: Saussure, Ferdinand de
stops.why: The other founder of semiotics; the Paris Review saw 'critical studies of Saussure' on the shelves.

stops.title: Prolegomena to a Theory of Language
stops.author: Hjelmslev, Louis
stops.why: Hjelmslev's expression/content planes are the formal core of A Theory of Semiotics.

stops.title: Du sens
stops.author: Greimas, Algirdas Julien
stops.why: Greimas's generative semiotics, the interlocutor of Lector in fabula.

stops.title: An Essay concerning Human Understanding
stops.author: Locke, John
stops.why: Named with Aristotle and Aquinas as an influence ('Joyce and Borges, certainly, but also Aristotle, Thomas Aquinas, John Locke'); Eco owned the 1690 first edition.

stops.title: Clavis universalis
stops.author: Rossi, Paolo
stops.why: The Italian study of Lullism and memory arts that Eco follows in The Search for the Perfect Language.

stops.title: Finnegans Wake
stops.author: Joyce, James
stops.why: The 'open work' par excellence in Opera aperta and Le poetiche di Joyce; Bologna holds Eco's Joyce studies shelf (Atherton's Books at the Wake, Anna Livia Plurabelle).

stops.title: Finnegans Wake

stops.why: The 'open work' par excellence in Opera aperta and Le poetiche di Joyce; Bologna holds Eco's Joyce studies shelf (Atherton's Books at the Wake, Anna Livia Plurabelle).

stops.author: Bruyne, Edgar de
stops.why: The standard history on which Eco's Arte e bellezza nell'estetica medievale rests.

stops.title: Rationale divinorum officiorum
stops.author: Durandus, Guillelmus
stops.why: The great medieval treatise on liturgical symbolism; Eco's first shelfmark in the incunabula section (1480).

stops.title: De laudibus sanctae crucis
stops.author: Hrabanus Maurus
stops.why: The carmina figurata of the Carolingian age, pattern-poems in praise of the Cross printed in red and black; Eco owned the 1503 Pforzheim edition.

stops.title: Sylvie
stops.author: Nerval, Gérard de
stops.why: The story Eco read 'countless times', translated into Italian (1999) and dissected in Six Walks and 'The Mists of the Valois'; the Braidense holds his translation and the 1854 Filles du feu.

stops.title: The Bible (Vulgate)
stops.why: Apocalypse, Song of Songs, John's prologue are collaged into The Name of the Rose; Eco owned a 1758 Vulgate.

stops.title: Les Soirées de Saint-Pétersbourg
stops.author: Maistre, Joseph de
stops.why: De Maistre's reactionary providentialism, and the theory of language he sets out in these dialogues, are the subject of Eco's essay 'The Linguistics of Joseph de Maistre'; Eco owned the 1821 first edition.

stops.title: La piazza universale di tutte le professioni del mondo
stops.author: Garzoni, Tomaso
stops.why: Garzoni's encyclopaedic catalogues of professions, madmen and 'cervelli' are Eco's favourite Renaissance list-makers (Vertigine della lista); seven Braidense records.

stops.title: Fasciculus temporum
stops.author: Rolevinck, Werner
stops.why: The illustrated universal chronicle-as-timeline, an early 'list of everything'; 1490 and 1512 editions owned.

stops.title: Supplementum chronicarum
stops.author: Foresti, Jacopo Filippo (da Bergamo)
stops.why: Universal chronicle, 1486 Venice incunable; part of the chronicle/list cluster of the earliest books.

stops.title: Manuel du libraire et de l'amateur de livres
stops.author: Brunet, Jacques-Charles
stops.why: The bibliophile's bible, the working tool Eco names in his bibliophilia essays; 1965-66 reprint in the rare room.

stops.title: Bibliotheca Philosophica Hermetica / Ritman Library catalogues
stops.author: Gilly, Carlos (ed.)
stops.why: The Amsterdam hermetic library's catalogues (Paracelsus, Hermes Trismegistus, Rosicrucians) form the reference shelf ECO.01.0254 next to the originals.

stops.title: John Dee's Library Catalogue
stops.author: Roberts, Julian & Watson, Andrew G. (eds.)
stops.why: A library-of-a-library: the catalogue of Dee's books shelved beside Dee's own works.

stops.title: De omnibus ingeniis augendae memoriae

stops.why: Trattato di mnemotecnica: uno dei filoni collezionistici della raccolta (alchimia, fisiognomica, mnemotecnica, p. 10) (Nuovo & Coletto 2022, no. 3, ISTC ia00210000)

C'e' tutta una storia...' (Non sperate di liberarvi dei libri, p. 99-100; nota 15) (Nuovo & Coletto 2022, no. 9, ISTC ia01208000)

Geografia antica, legata con il Pomponio Mela che Nuovo e Coletto contano fra le fonti dell'Isola del giorno prima (p. 10) (Nuovo & Coletto 2022, no. 13, ISTC id00254000)

stops.title: Artes orandi, epistolandi, memorandi
