quotes_general.text: if the library is, as Borges would have it, a model of the Universe, let us try to turn it into a universe on a human scale, and, I recall, on a human scale also means cheerful, even with the possibility of a cappuccino
quotes_general.text_it: se la biblioteca è, come vuole Borges, un modello dell'Universo, cerchiamo di trasformarla in un universo a misura d'uomo, e, ricordo, a misura d'uomo vuol dire anche gaio, anche con la possibilità del cappuccino
quotes_general.speaker: Umberto Eco
quotes_general.source: Umberto Eco, De Bibliotheca, lecture given 10 March 1981 at Palazzo Sormani for the 25th anniversary of the Biblioteca Comunale di Milano (Milano: Biblioteca Comunale, 'I quaderni di Palazzo Sormani', 1981; repr. in Sette anni di desiderio, Bompiani 1983)
quotes_general.context: Closing of the 1981 lecture, after the 21-point 'negative model' of the bad library.

quotes_general.text: Our risk is a loss of memory through an excess, by now, of artificial memory. I press a button and a bibliography of ten thousand titles arrives; with a bibliography of ten thousand titles I do nothing, I take the bibliography and throw it away. Once I went to the library, I found three books, but at least I read those three books and managed to say something; now with ten thousand I no longer read them. So there, you see, where we believe we have conquered an immense memory, we have lost it.
quotes_general.text_it: Il nostro rischio è di una perdita di memoria per eccesso, ormai, di memoria artificiale. Schiaccio un bottone e mi arriva una bibliografia di diecimila titoli; con una bibliografia di diecimila titoli io non faccio niente, prendo la bibliografia e la butto via. Una volta andavo in biblioteca, trovavo tre libri, ma almeno tre libri li leggevo e riuscivo a dire qualcosa; adesso con diecimila non li leggo più. Allora ecco, vede, lì dove noi crediamo di avere conquistato una memoria immensa, l'abbiamo perduta.
quotes_general.speaker: Umberto Eco
quotes_general.source: Davide Ferrario (dir.), 'Umberto Eco. La biblioteca del mondo' (Rossofuoco / Fandango, 2022, 80 min), Italian auto-captions of the unofficial upload (caption time 00:26:10)
quotes_general.context: The same argument appears in the Bustina di Minerva of 2000 cited by AIB Notizie ('riceve una bibliografia di diecimila titoli, e rinuncia'). Final word 'persa' inferred from context (caption cuts at 'l'abbiamo').

quotes_general.text: There remains that great majority who do not read because they have no intellectual curiosity. To have intellectual curiosity means to be alive, and mind you, there aren't that many people alive in the world.
quotes_general.text_it: Rimane quella grande maggioranza che non legge perché non ha curiosità intellettuali. Avere curiosità intellettuali vuol dire essere vivi, e guardi che c'è mica tanta gente viva al mondo.
quotes_general.speaker: Umberto Eco
quotes_general.source: Davide Ferrario (dir.), 'Umberto Eco. La biblioteca del mondo' (Rossofuoco / Fandango, 2022, 80 min), Italian auto-captions of the unofficial upload (caption time 00:41:01)
quotes_general.context: Archival interview; quoted on the Film Forum page as 'To be intellectually curious is to be alive. And believe me, a lot of people are not alive.'

quotes_general.text: For the labyrinth of the library I designed, I don't know, 50, 60 different labyrinths, studying all the existing labyrinths.
quotes_general.source: Writer Umberto Eco: I Was Always Narrating | Louisiana Channel
quotes_general.speaker: Umberto Eco

quotes_general.text: Sometimes, on the contrary, you have to walk through libraries or to places -- places for me is very important -- to visit the places.
quotes_general.source: Writer Umberto Eco: I Was Always Narrating | Louisiana Channel
quotes_general.speaker: Umberto Eco

quotes_general.text: So I don't have Galileo Galilei but I have Ptolemy, because it was wrong about the movement of the Earth.
quotes_general.source: Writer Umberto Eco: I Was Always Narrating | Louisiana Channel
quotes_general.speaker: Umberto Eco

quotes_general.text: All together in different places there should be about 50,000.
quotes_general.source: Writer Umberto Eco: I Was Always Narrating | Louisiana Channel
quotes_general.speaker: Umberto Eco

quotes_general.text: Here, when I arrived 25 years ago there were 30,000, but since, many of them... I have no more time to count them, but I think there are 35,000.
quotes_general.source: Writer Umberto Eco: I Was Always Narrating | Louisiana Channel
quotes_general.speaker: Umberto Eco

quotes_general.text: [Interviewer:] Do you have time to read a lot? [Eco:] Another provocative way to answer such a question is: I don't read -- I write.
quotes_general.source: Writer Umberto Eco: I Was Always Narrating | Louisiana Channel
quotes_general.speaker: Umberto Eco

quotes_general.text: There is a cursory reading -- not the quick reading of which... once Woody Allen said: 'I am using the quick reading -- I read "War and Peace" -- he speaks of Russia.'
quotes_general.source: Writer Umberto Eco: I Was Always Narrating | Louisiana Channel
quotes_general.speaker: Umberto Eco

quotes_general.text: There are my books -- translations and... From there to... and they are books on me.
quotes_general.source: Writer Umberto Eco: I Was Always Narrating | Louisiana Channel
quotes_general.speaker: Umberto Eco

rooms.name: Living room
rooms.blurb: Modern furnishings, the Castello Sforzesco in the windows, glass display cases with open antique illustrated books, seashells and rare comics, a lute and recorders (parisreview-2008, zanni-photo-2010). In 2022 the guided visit started here: art books, "libri da esposizione", encyclopaedias and atlases, and the vitrine in which Eco displayed the books of his current research (criticaletteraria-2022). The plaster statue and the three vitrines stand on the W wall beside the vestibule door, the cases 1.2 m out from the wall with the credenza and the dining table behind them, the curiosity cabinet and a second door on the E wall, the piano on the door wall; no wall of library books is in the room (bookcase E stands in the art corridor).

seen_in_film.label: Wooden cabinet of curiosities
seen_in_film.description: 19th-century pine/walnut dresser-bookcase ~2.2 m wide x 2.6 m high: glazed upper cupboards, open middle shelves, panelled cupboards below. Filled with objects (see o38-o40): gilt bronze foot, typographic drawer, white faceted panel, glass and wooden spheres on stands, ostrich and emu eggs, wooden clock, oval-framed sepia family photographs, silver bell, bat skeleton in an acrylic box, terracotta head, bottles of coloured sand, a nun/Madonna doll, clock movement. A large flat-screen TV on a stand is beside it; a floor lamp in front.

seen_in_film.label: Objects on the wooden cabinet, middle shelf
seen_in_film.description: Left to right on the open shelf: a gilt bronze cast of a right foot; a white typographic drawer (4x4 compartments) holding black cylinders; a large white faceted panel; a glass sphere on a turned stand; a dark wooden sphere (globe) on a stand; an ostrich egg on a black stand; a wooden mantel clock with a small dial; a dark emu egg in a glass; a wooden ball on a black block.

seen_in_film.label: Family photographs and small silver on the wooden cabinet
seen_in_film.description: Lower shelf: eight oval gilt-framed sepia photographs (19th/early-20th-c. family portraits) hung on the back panel, two larger square-framed daguerreotype-style portraits, a silver repousse frame, a silver hand bell, a small silver box, a silver dish, a framed photo of a group, and a figurine in a glass frame of a bearded man with round glasses playing a recorder (an Eco caricature puppet).

seen_in_film.label: Curiosities in the upper cabinet
seen_in_film.description: Upper open bays and glazed parts: a terracotta classical female head; a gilt bronze disc relief (Pomodoro-style); a cracked ostrich egg on a black stand; four glass bottles of layered coloured sand; stacked small wooden boxes; a wooden cigar press; a leather case; a snuff box; a small book 'Gunga Din'; a carved terracotta grotesque; a bat skeleton mounted in a clear acrylic box; a pocket stopwatch; a wooden hat-block; a carved wooden nun/Madonna figure with veil; a clock mechanism (gears) behind glass.

seen_in_film.label: Bat skeleton in a glass case
seen_in_film.description: Mounted skeleton of a bat with spread wings in a small glass box.

seen_in_film.label: Polychrome wooden bust of a female saint
seen_in_film.description: Old carved and painted bust of a veiled woman (nun/Madonna) inside the glazed section.

seen_in_film.label: Small religious panel painting
seen_in_film.description: Gold-ground devotional painting (Madonna with figures) inside the glazed compartment.

seen_in_film.label: Pocket watch and hedgehog figure

quotes.text: The library really is the symbol and the reality of a collective memory.
quotes.text_it: La biblioteca è effettivamente simbolo e realtà di una memoria collettiva.
quotes.source: Umberto Eco. La biblioteca del mondo (Davide Ferrario, 2022)
quotes.speaker: Umberto Eco
quotes.context: Interview in the study, 2015 (black and white), used over the opening long take

quotes.text: Vegetal memory, since books are unfortunately made of wood nowadays, and once of papyrus and so on: vegetal memory is the memory of books.
quotes.text_it: La memoria vegetale, visto che i libri si fanno ormai col legno, ma una volta anche col papiro: la memoria vegetale è quella dei libri.
quotes.source: Umberto Eco. La biblioteca del mondo (Davide Ferrario, 2022)
quotes.speaker: Umberto Eco

quotes.text: The visitor comes in and says: "So many books! Have you read them all?" At first I thought the remark betrayed only people with little familiarity with books, used to seeing small shelves holding five detective novels and a children's encyclopaedia in instalments. But experience has taught me that the remark is uttered even by people above suspicion. One can say that they are still people who think of the shelf as a store of books already read and not of the library as a working tool, but that is not enough. I believe that in front of many books anyone is seized by the anguish of knowledge, and fatally slides towards the question that expresses his torment and his remorse.
quotes.text_it: Il visitatore entra e dice: "Quanti libri! Li ha letti tutti?" All'inizio ritenevo che la frase rivelasse solo persone di scarsa dimestichezza con il libro, aduse a vedere solo scaffaletti con cinque gialli e una enciclopedia dei ragazzi a dispense. Ma l'esperienza mi ha insegnato che la frase viene pronunciata anche da persone insospettabili. Si può dire che si tratta pur sempre di persone che hanno una nozione dello scaffale come deposito di libri letti e non della biblioteca come strumento di lavoro, ma non basta. Ritengo che di fronte a molti libri chiunque sia preso dall'angoscia della conoscenza, e fatalmente scivoli verso la domanda che esprime il suo tormento e i suoi rimorsi.
quotes.source: Umberto Eco, 'Come giustificare una biblioteca privata', in Il secondo diario minimo (Milano: Bompiani, 1992) [first published as a 'Bustina di Minerva', L'Espresso, 1990]
quotes.speaker: Umberto Eco
quotes.context: Opening of the library section of the essay; establishes the library as 'strumento di lavoro' (working tool) rather than a deposit of read books.

quotes.text: I once adopted the contemptuous answer: "I haven't read any of them, otherwise why would I keep them here?" But it is a dangerous answer because it triggers the obvious reaction: "And where do you put the ones you have read?" Better is Roberto Leydi's standard answer: "Many more, sir, many more", which freezes the adversary and plunges him into a state of stupefied veneration. But I find it merciless and anxiety-inducing. Now I have fallen back on the statement: "No, these are the ones I have to read by next month, the others I keep at the university", an answer that on the one hand suggests a sublime ergonomic strategy, and on the other induces the visitor to hasten the moment of leave-taking.
quotes.text_it: Io un tempo avevo adottato la risposta sprezzante: "Non ne ho letto nessuno, altrimenti perché li terrei qui?" Ma è una risposta pericolosa perché scatena l'ovvia reazione: "E dove mette quelli che ha letto?" Migliore è la risposta standard di Roberto Leydi: "Molti di più, signore, molti di più", che gela l'avversario e lo piomba in uno stato di stuporosa venerazione. Ma la trovo impietosa e ansiogena. Ora ho ripiegato verso l'affermazione: "No, questi sono quelli che debbo leggere entro il mese prossimo, gli altri li tengo all'università", risposta che da un lato suggerisce una sublime strategia ergonomica, e dall'altro induce il visitatore ad anticipare il momento del congedo.
quotes.source: Umberto Eco, 'Come giustificare una biblioteca privata', in Il secondo diario minimo (Milano: Bompiani, 1992) [first published as a 'Bustina di Minerva', L'Espresso, 1990]
quotes.speaker: Umberto Eco
quotes.context: The canonical three answers. Roberto Leydi was an ethnomusicologist and friend of Eco.

quotes.text: In the past I adopted a tone of contemptuous sarcasm. 'I haven't read any of them; otherwise, why would I keep them here?' But this is a dangerous answer because it invites the obvious follow-up: 'And where do you put them after you've read them?' The best answer is the one always used by Roberto Leydi: 'And more, dear sir, many more,' which freezes the adversary and plunges him into a state of awed admiration. But I find it merciless and angst-generating. Now I have fallen back upon the riposte: 'No, these are the ones I have to read by the end of the month. I keep the others in my office,' a reply that on the one hand suggests a sublime ergonomic strategy, and on the other hand leads the visitor to hasten the moment of his departure.
quotes.source: Umberto Eco, 'How to Justify a Private Library', in How to Travel with a Salmon & Other Essays, trans. William Weaver (San Diego: Harcourt, 1994), p. 117
quotes.speaker: Umberto Eco
quotes.context: William Weaver's published English version of q02; 'by the end of the month' and 'in my office' differ slightly from the Italian ('entro il mese prossimo', 'all'università').

quotes.text: Naturally the bibliophile, even one who collects contemporary books, is exposed to the snare of the imbecile who walks into your house, sees all those shelves, and pronounces: "So many books! Have you read them all?" Daily experience tells us that this question is asked even by people with a more than satisfactory IQ. Faced with this outrage there exist, to my knowledge, three standard answers. The first stops the visitor and cuts off all relations: "I haven't read any of them, otherwise why would I keep them here?" But it gratifies the intruder by tickling his sense of superiority and I don't see why we should do him that favour. The second plunges the intruder into a state of inferiority, and goes: "More, sir, many more!" The third is a variation on the second and I use it when I want the visitor to fall prey to painful astonishment. "No," I tell him, "the ones I have already read I keep at the university; these are the ones I have to read by next week."
quotes.text_it: Naturalmente il bibliofilo, anche chi colleziona libri contemporanei, è esposto all'insidia dell'imbecille che ti entra in casa, vede tutti quegli scaffali, e pronuncia: "Quanti libri! Li ha letti tutti?" L'esperienza quotidiana ci dice che questa domanda viene fatta anche da persone dal quoziente intellettivo più che soddisfacente. Di fronte a questo oltraggio esistono, a mia scienza, tre risposte standard. La prima blocca il visitatore e interrompe ogni rapporto, ed è: "Non ne ho letto nessuno, altrimenti perché li terrei qui?" Essa però gratifica l'importuno solleticando il suo senso di superiorità e non vedo perché si debba rendergli questo favore. La seconda risposta piomba l'importuno in uno stato d'inferiorità, e suona: "Di più, signore, molti di più!" La terza è una variazione della seconda e la uso quando voglio che il visitatore cada in preda a doloroso stupore. "No," gli dico, "quelli che ho già letto li tengo all'università, questi sono quelli che debbo leggere entro la settimana prossima."
quotes.source: Umberto Eco, lectio magistralis at the Fiera Internazionale del Libro di Torino, May 2007 (published as 'La memoria vegetale', in La memoria vegetale e altri scritti di bibliofilia, Rovello 2007 / Bompiani 2011)
quotes.speaker: Umberto Eco
quotes.context: Eco's later (2007) rewriting of the three answers; here the deadline is 'next week'. The same passage is voiced in Ferrario's 2022 film (see che-fare.com review).

quotes.text: A home library is not only a place where books are gathered: it is also a place that reads them on our behalf.
quotes.text_it: Una biblioteca di casa non è solo un luogo in cui si raccolgono libri: è anche un luogo che li legge per conto nostro.
quotes.source: Umberto Eco, as quoted in Rivista Studio, 'Comprare libri per non leggerli' (6 February 2017)
quotes.speaker: Umberto Eco
quotes.context: Rivista Studio quotes the sentence in these words from a lectio magistralis of Eco's; AIB Notizie attributes a variant ('Una biblioteca non si limita a raccogliere i tuoi libri, li legge anche per conto tuo') to a Bustina di Minerva in L'Espresso (1998); the underlying argument (you absorb unread books by handling, dusting and cross-reading) is in the essays of La memoria vegetale. Neither primary text has been read.

quotes.text: The writer Umberto Eco belongs to that small class of scholars who are encyclopedic, insightful, and nondull. He is the owner of a large personal library (containing thirty thousand books), and separates visitors into two categories: those who react with "Wow! Signore professore dottore Eco, what a library you have! How many of these books have you read?" and the others—a very small minority—who get the point that a private library is not an ego-boosting appendage but a research tool. Read books are far less valuable than unread ones. The library should contain as much of what you do not know as your financial means, mortgage rates, and the currently tight real-estate market allows you to put there. You will accumulate more knowledge and more books as you grow older, and the growing number of unread books on the shelves will look at you menacingly. Indeed, the more you know, the larger the rows of unread books. Let us call this collection of unread books an antilibrary.
quotes.source: Nassim Nicholas Taleb, The Black Swan: The Impact of the Highly Improbable (New York: Random House, 2007), Prologue / ch. 1 'Umberto Eco's Antilibrary, or How We Seek Validation'
quotes.speaker: Nassim Nicholas Taleb
quotes.context: The passage that coined 'antilibrary'; Taleb's 'thirty thousand' refers to the Milan flat only.

quotes.text: There are several ways of responding to the person who comes to your house, notices your impressive library and can only think to ask, 'Have you read them all?' One of my friends used to say, 'And more, my dear sir, and more.' Personally, I've two replies. The first: 'No. These are just the books I'm planning to read next week. The ones I've already read are at the university.' The second: 'I haven't read any of these books. Why would I keep them, otherwise?'
quotes.source: Umberto Eco and Jean-Claude Carrière, This Is Not the End of the Book (conversation curated by Jean-Philippe de Tonnac, trans. Polly McLean, Harvill Secker, London 2011; orig. N'espérez pas vous débarrasser des livres, 2009 / Non sperate di liberarvi dei libri, Bompiani 2009), chapter 'All the books we haven't read'
quotes.speaker: Umberto Eco
quotes.context: Eco's 2009 conversational retelling of the three answers.

quotes.text: There are more books in the world than hours in which to read them. And that doesn't just apply to all the books ever published, but even to only the most important books of a particular culture. We are thus deeply influenced by books that we haven't read, that we haven't had the time to read. Who has actually read Finnegans Wake — I mean from beginning to end? Who has read the Bible properly, from Genesis to the Apocalypse? If I were to combine all the sections I've read, I could boast of about one-third. But no more. And yet I've a fairly accurate notion of what I haven't read.
quotes.source: Umberto Eco and Jean-Claude Carrière, This Is Not the End of the Book (conversation curated by Jean-Philippe de Tonnac, trans. Polly McLean, Harvill Secker, London 2011; orig. N'espérez pas vous débarrasser des livres, 2009 / Non sperate di liberarvi dei libri, Bompiani 2009), chapter 'All the books we haven't read'
quotes.speaker: Umberto Eco
quotes.context: Eco on Pierre Bayard and the books one knows without having read them; he adds that he owns three editions of the Mahabharata in three languages and has never read it.

rooms.name: Room of the Ancients (rare-book room)
rooms.blurb: A small all-wood room with a balcony on the Castello Sforzesco, no telephone or computer, flutes and scores, the books shelved next to mirabilia - dog testicles in formalin, shells, coral, wooden models (ansa-2022, breraplus-idea, zanni-2010); the family recalls its original shape as elliptical, whereas the Braidense Studiolo that reproduces it is rectangular (rivista-studio-2022). It held the Bibliotheca semiologica curiosa lunatica magica et pneumatica, 1,328 volumes at the transfer of August 2021 (carriere-2011, braidense-opac, aib-2022). Braidense's catalogue documents the transferred collection and its ordering: the running number of a shelfmark records the order the volumes had in the author's home, ECO.01 the books on the shelves of the room, ECO.02 the books kept elsewhere in it (on the desk, for example), ECO.03 the most precious books. Its additional ECO.04 section brings together publications by Eco for research and does not by itself establish a copy's original position in the Milan apartment (braidense-studiolo-2022, p. 6).

It held the Bibliotheca semiologica curiosa lunatica magica et pneumatica, 1,328 volumes at the transfer of August 2021 (carriere-2011, braidense-opac, aib-2022). Braidense's catalogue documents the transferred collection and its ordering: the running number of a shelfmark records the order the volumes had in the author's home, ECO.01 the books on the shelves of the room, ECO.02 the books kept elsewhere in it (on the desk, for example), ECO.03 the most precious books. Its additional ECO.04 section brings together publications by Eco for research and does not by itself establish a copy's original position in the Milan apartment (braidense-studiolo-2022, p. 6).

rooms.catalog_note: Braidense ECO.xx shelfmarks (2,105 records in the export; the library counted 1,328 volumes at the transfer, and a record is not a volume: set records stand behind their volumes, works bound together share a shelfmark): ECO.01 the books on the shelves of the room (c. 1,570 records / 997 running numbers used up to 1107: hermetica, Kircher, Fludd, Rosicrucians, curiosa; median year 1719); ECO.02 the books kept elsewhere in the room, on the desk for example (372 records / 165 numbers to 169: 19th-c. French sets, Dumas, Sue, Peladan, "fous litteraires"; median 1856); ECO.03 the most precious books (51 records / 37 numbers to 77: Dee 1564, Bruno 1582, Khunrath 1609, Locke 1690 alongside incunabula; median 1563; all 36 incunabula of the AIB Studi 2022 list are in the Braidense records: 19 under ECO.03 and 17 under ECO.01); ECO.04 the library's own reference section of Eco's publications (110 records / 102 numbers; Italian editions 1975-2025, most of them inventoried by the Braidense between 1996 and 2016, the rest from 2022 on): not a shelf of the flat, so its records are listed as reference entries and drawn on no cabinet. At 30-40 volumes per metre the three shelved runs need about 25-33 m + 6-8 m + 1-2.5 m = c. 32-44 shelf metres; the two wall units drawn below offer c. 80 m, consistent with loosely shelved folios and the mirabilia between them.

film_notes.description: Small high-ceilinged room (~6.5 x 3.6 m; family says originally elliptical) with a French window and wrought-iron balcony looking straight at the corner tower of the Castello Sforzesco. Both long walls: cherry-wood glazed bookcases with a band of drawers/cupboards at waist height, folios and vellum quartos behind glass, mirabilia between the books. Centre: long dark oak table with leather inset and six cane-seat chairs. End wall opposite the balcony: white wall with framed engravings, the door to the vestibule (white shelving and coat hooks visible beyond it). Cognac leather armchair and yellow-shaded floor lamp by the balcony; small round tripod side table; music stand with score and recorder; pendant lamp on a ceiling rail; radiator under the balcony door.

quotes.text: Recently someone asked me why I collect only false books and not true ones: because they are more beautiful. To prove Pythagoras' theorem two drawings will do; to prove false theories, alchemical ones, illustrations come out.
quotes.text_it: Recentemente qualcuno mi chiedeva perché colleziono solo libri falsi e non veri: perché sono più belli. Se devi dimostrare il teorema di Pitagora con due disegni hai fatto tutto; se devi dimostrare delle teorie false, alchemiche, vengono fuori delle illustrazioni.
quotes.source: Umberto Eco. La biblioteca del mondo (Davide Ferrario, 2022)
quotes.speaker: Umberto Eco

quotes.text: I am a rare books collector too. And my collection concerns only fake books, books that say the contrary: so I don't have Galileo Galilei, but I have Ptolemy, because it was wrong about the movement of the Earth.
quotes.source: Louisiana Channel, Writer Umberto Eco: I Was Always Narrating (2015)
quotes.speaker: Umberto Eco
quotes.context: Louisiana Channel interview

quotes.text: And now, to reply to your question, I only possess about thirty incunabula, though they do include what you might call the 'essentials'. For instance, the Hypnerotomachia Poliphili, the Nuremberg Chronicle, Ficino's translation of the Corpus Hermeticum, the Arbor Vitae Crucifixae Jesu Christi by Ubertino Da Casale (who became one of the characters in my Name of the Rose), and so on. My collection is very focused. It is a Bibliotheca Semiologica Curiosa Lunatica Magica et Pneumatica, or 'a collection dedicated to the occult and mistaken sciences'. For example, I have Ptolemy, who was wrong about the movement of the Earth, but not Galileo, who was right.
quotes.source: Umberto Eco and Jean-Claude Carrière, This Is Not the End of the Book (conversation curated by Jean-Philippe de Tonnac, trans. Polly McLean, Harvill Secker, London 2011; orig. N'espérez pas vous débarrasser des livres, 2009 / Non sperate di liberarvi dei libri, Bompiani 2009), chapter on incunabula ('Tell me about your collection')
quotes.speaker: Umberto Eco
quotes.context: Eco's own gloss of the collection's name. The Braidense fund actually counts 36 incunabula (AIB Studi 2022).

quotes.text: I have only about thirty incunabula but I certainly have the ones a collector cannot do without (the incontournables, as it is fashionable to say in France today, the ones you cannot get around) […]. My collection is very focused. It is a Bibliotheca semiologica curiosa lunatica magica et pneumatica, in other words a collection devoted to occult knowledge and false knowledge. I have Ptolemy, who was wrong about the motion of the Earth, but not Galileo, who was right.
quotes.text_it: Io ho solo una trentina di incunaboli ma ho certamente quelli di cui un collezionista non può fare a meno (gli incontournables, come va di moda dire oggi in Francia, quelli a cui non puoi girare intorno) […]. La mia collezione è molto orientata. Si tratta di una Bibliotheca semiologica curiosa lunatica magica et pneumatica, detto altrimenti di una collezione dedicata al sapere occulto e al sapere falso. Ho Tolomeo, che si sbagliava sul moto della Terra, ma non ho Galileo, che aveva ragione.
quotes.source: Umberto Eco in conversation with Jean-Claude Carrière, Non sperate di liberarvi dei libri (Milano: Bompiani, 2009), p. 112, as quoted in Angela Nuovo and Aldo Coletto, 'Gli incunaboli di Umberto Eco', AIB studi 62 (2022)
quotes.speaker: Umberto Eco
quotes.context: Italian edition wording of q11; 'sapere occulto e sapere falso' is the phrase the Fondazione and Braidense reuse ('occult knowledge and false learning').

quotes.text: I have all his books except the Ars Magnesia, which is impossible to get hold of, despite being a small book with no illustrations. Kircher wasn't yet known at the time of publication, so I expect only a few copies were printed. Also, the book is so devoid of charm that probably no one thought it worth saving. But I also possess the works of Robert Fludd and a fair few other eccentric minds.
quotes.source: Umberto Eco and Jean-Claude Carrière, This Is Not the End of the Book (conversation curated by Jean-Philippe de Tonnac, trans. Polly McLean, Harvill Secker, London 2011; orig. N'espérez pas vous débarrasser des livres, 2009 / Non sperate di liberarvi dei libri, Bompiani 2009), chapter on incunabula (answering Carrière on Athanasius Kircher)
quotes.speaker: Umberto Eco
quotes.context: On Kircher and Fludd; Eco adds that collectors prize Kircher for 'the exceptional beauty of his books' and that he taught a 1992 course on Kircher's reading of hieroglyphs.

quotes.text: I am fascinated by error, by bad faith and idiocy. Like Flaubert. You and I both adore silliness. In Faith in Fakes I describe visiting American museums that show reproductions of art works, including a waxwork Venus de Milo with arms. In The Limits of Interpretation I create a theory of fakes and forgeries. With regard to my novels, Foucault's Pendulum was inspired by occultists who believe feverishly in everything, whereas the main character in Baudolino is a delightful and, in the end, benevolent charlatan.
quotes.source: Umberto Eco and Jean-Claude Carrière, This Is Not the End of the Book (conversation curated by Jean-Philippe de Tonnac, trans. Polly McLean, Harvill Secker, London 2011; orig. N'espérez pas vous débarrasser des livres, 2009 / Non sperate di liberarvi dei libri, Bompiani 2009) (Carrière: 'And how do you explain this bizarre choice?')
quotes.speaker: Umberto Eco
quotes.context: Why the collection is devoted to error and forgery.

quotes.text: I think people often confuse a collection of books that one owns with a collection of ancient books. I have 50,000 books in my various homes. But these are modern books. I also have 1,200 rare titles. There's another difference, too. The ancient books are books I have chosen and paid for, whereas the modern ones are made up not only of the books I have bought over the years, but also, and increasingly, those that people have sent me as tributes. I give lots of them to my students, but I do keep a fair few, and that's how I've got to 50,000.
quotes.source: Umberto Eco and Jean-Claude Carrière, This Is Not the End of the Book (conversation curated by Jean-Philippe de Tonnac, trans. Polly McLean, Harvill Secker, London 2011; orig. N'espérez pas vous débarrasser des livres, 2009 / Non sperate di liberarvi dei libri, Bompiani 2009) (de Tonnac: 'How large are your collections?')
quotes.speaker: Umberto Eco
quotes.context: The 50,000 / 1,200 figures Eco himself used from about 2008 on.

quotes.text: I obviously wouldn't want my collection to be dispersed. My family could give it to a public library, or else sell it through an auction house, which would mean the collection would go to a university intact. That's all I care about.
quotes.source: Umberto Eco and Jean-Claude Carrière, This Is Not the End of the Book (conversation curated by Jean-Philippe de Tonnac, trans. Polly McLean, Harvill Secker, London 2011; orig. N'espérez pas vous débarrasser des livres, 2009 / Non sperate di liberarvi dei libri, Bompiani 2009), chapter 'What will happen to your library after you die?'
quotes.speaker: Umberto Eco
quotes.context: What actually happened: the rare books went to the state (Braidense, 2018/2021), the modern library on 90-year loan to Bologna (2026).

quotes.text: I don't know if mine is an accurate reflection of me. As I've said, I collect books whose contents I don't believe, so it must be more like a mirror image. Or perhaps a reflection of my contradictory nature. I'm not sure, because I don't show my collection to many people. A book collection is a solitary, masturbatory kind of phenomenon, and you don't often come across people who share your passions. If you own beautiful paintings, people come over to admire them. But no one is sincerely interested in your collection of old books.
quotes.source: Umberto Eco and Jean-Claude Carrière, This Is Not the End of the Book (conversation curated by Jean-Philippe de Tonnac, trans. Polly McLean, Harvill Secker, London 2011; orig. N'espérez pas vous débarrasser des livres, 2009 / Non sperate di liberarvi dei libri, Bompiani 2009)
quotes.speaker: Umberto Eco
quotes.context: Matches the family's account that only a few friends were admitted to the Stanza degli antichi.

quotes.text: Having spoken so passionately in favour of books, I had better admit that the first thing I would save is my 250-gigabyte hard drive, which contains all my writing from the last thirty years. After that, if there were still time, I would of course try to save one of my oldest books — not necessarily the most valuable, but the one I love the most. But how to choose? I am extremely attached to lots of them. I would hope not to have too long to deliberate. Perhaps I would take Bernhard von Breydenbach's Peregrinatio in Terram Sanctam, Spier, Drach, 1490, on account of its wonderful illustrated plates on several folded pages.
quotes.source: Umberto Eco and Jean-Claude Carrière, This Is Not the End of the Book (conversation curated by Jean-Philippe de Tonnac, trans. Polly McLean, Harvill Secker, London 2011; orig. N'espérez pas vous débarrasser des livres, 2009 / Non sperate di liberarvi dei libri, Bompiani 2009) (Carrière: 'Your house is on fire — what would you save first?')
quotes.speaker: Umberto Eco
quotes.context: The fire question. Elsewhere in the book: 'It's no accident that I wrote a book about a library burning down. I'm always worrying about it happening to my house' (the fire chief lived upstairs when he was a child).

quotes.text: I own a total of about fifty thousand books. But as a rare books collector I am fascinated by the human propensity for deviating thought. So I collect books about subjects in which I don't believe, like kabbalah, alchemy, magic, invented languages. Books that lie, albeit unwittingly. I have Ptolemy, not Galileo, because Galileo told the truth. I prefer lunatic science.
quotes.source: Lila Azam Zanganeh, 'Umberto Eco, The Art of Fiction No. 197', The Paris Review 185 (Summer 2008)
quotes.speaker: Umberto Eco
quotes.context: Answer to 'Your library here in Milan is a legend in and of itself. What kind of books do you like to collect?'

quotes.text: I receive an enormous quantity of books every day—novels, new editions of books I already own—so every single week I fill up some boxes and send them off to my university, where there is a big table with a sign that says take a book and run.
quotes.source: Lila Azam Zanganeh, 'Umberto Eco, The Art of Fiction No. 197', The Paris Review 185 (Summer 2008)
quotes.speaker: Umberto Eco
quotes.context: Answer to 'Do you ever give books away?'

quotes.text: Semiological, curious, lunatic, magical and pneumatic library.
quotes.text_it: Bibliotheca semiologica curiosa lunatica magica et pneumatica.
quotes.source: Davide Ferrario (dir.), 'Umberto Eco. La biblioteca del mondo' (Rossofuoco / Fandango, 2022, 80 min), Italian auto-captions of the unofficial upload (caption time 00:06:18)

quotes.text: These ones Dad never used. Well, books have to be touched, you know, with your hands.
quotes.text_it: Questi papà non li usava mai. Beh, i libri vanno toccati, insomma, con le mani.
quotes.source: Davide Ferrario (dir.), 'Umberto Eco. La biblioteca del mondo' (Rossofuoco / Fandango, 2022, 80 min), Italian auto-captions of the unofficial upload (caption time 00:07:40)
quotes.speaker: Carlotta Eco
quotes.context: Said while handling the old books (about gloves, apparently); consistent with Eco's 'toccare la carta che fa ancora crac crac sotto le dita' (Il Foglio 2022).

quotes.text: If papyri and manuscripts have survived for thousands of years and we have perfectly fresh books printed more than five hundred years ago, we do not know how long electronic media will survive. We do not know, because our present computers are no longer able to read what we recorded a few decades ago on palaeolithic floppy disks.
quotes.text_it: Se papiri e manoscritti sono sopravvissuti per migliaia di anni e disponiamo di libri freschissimi stampati più di cinquecento anni fa, non sappiamo quanto sopravvivano i supporti elettronici. Non lo sappiamo, perché i nostri computer attuali non sono più in grado di leggere quanto avevamo registrato qualche decennio fa sui paleolitici floppy disc.
quotes.source: Davide Ferrario (dir.), 'Umberto Eco. La biblioteca del mondo' (Rossofuoco / Fandango, 2022, 80 min), Italian auto-captions of the unofficial upload (caption time 00:20:58)
quotes.speaker: Umberto Eco
quotes.context: Eco text (from the 'Bustina di Minerva' / Carrière conversations) voiced in the film; also in the trailer clips (bcK8rOkcb3k 00:00:50).

quotes.text: I began in the 1970s to concern myself with the lie. In my Theory of Semiotics it is said that a sign is everything that can be used to lie, a definition that has enjoyed some success. From there came the interest in the fake. […] Then I had written an essay on how forgeries had influenced history: many forged documents have provoked great historical events, the Donation of Constantine, the letter of Prester John which drove the exploration first of Asia and then of Africa.
quotes.text_it: Ho cominciato negli anni Settanta a occuparmi della bugia. Nel mio Trattato di semiotica generale si dice che il segno è tutto ciò che può essere usato per mentire, una definizione che ha avuto qualche fortuna. Di lì l'interesse per il falso. […] Poi avevo scritto un saggio su come i falsi avevano influenzato la storia: molti documenti falsi hanno però provocato dei grandi avvenimenti storici, la donazione di Costantino, la lettera del Prete Gianni che ha spinto all'esplorazione prima dell'Asia e poi dell'Africa.
quotes.source: Davide Ferrario (dir.), 'Umberto Eco. La biblioteca del mondo' (Rossofuoco / Fandango, 2022, 80 min), Italian auto-captions of the unofficial upload (caption time 01:02:23)
quotes.speaker: Umberto Eco
quotes.context: The semiotic rationale for a library of 'books that lie'; Guardian 2011: 'From lies to forgeries the step is not so long, and I have written technical essays on the logic of forgeries and on the influence of forgeries on history.'

quotes.text: It was while I was working on Foucault's Pendulum that I started receiving the money from the translation of The Name of the Rose. And I decided to use it to buy these books. […] I have always been obsessed—also in my role as a scholar—with the problem of fakes and forgeries. […] This collection of books is my way to try to understand falsification and lies. […] There are no books by Galileo in my collection, but Ptolemy is there. Because Galileo told the truth, while poor old Ptolemy was in error.
quotes.source: Patricia Guy, 'The Parasitic Press: Umberto Eco', Publishers Weekly, 23 October 2015 (interview in Eco's Milan apartment)
quotes.speaker: Umberto Eco
quotes.context: Dates the start of the rare-book collection to the mid-1980s (Name of the Rose royalties); Eco also explains that 'semiologic, curiosity, lunatic, magic, and pneumatic' are 'the words used in antique catalogues to describe books that are about falsity and frauds'.

quotes.text: I am a subject collector and my collection is titled Bibliotheca semiologica curiosa, magica et pneumatica (a title derived from some famous handbooks such as Graesse's). I look for strange languages, from invented languages to alchemy, mnemonics and steganographies. Generally books that say what is false, which is why I have Ptolemy but not Galileo.
quotes.text_it: Sono un collezionista a soggetto e la mia raccolta si intitola Bibliotheca semiologica curiosa, magica et pneumatica (titolo derivato da alcuni manuali celebri come quello di Graesse). Cerco linguaggi strani, dalle lingue inventate all'alchimia, le mnemotecniche e le steganografie. In genere libri che dicano il falso, per cui ho Tolomeo ma non Galileo.
quotes.source: Umberto Eco, as quoted ('mi disse una volta Eco') in 'Il mondo di Eco in una stanza', Corriere del Ticino, 26 June 2022
quotes.speaker: Umberto Eco
quotes.context: The newspaper prints the title as 'Biliotheca'; the collection's name is given here as Eco wrote it.

quotes.text: A bibliophile's pleasure is to pore over catalogues, to collate, to keep updating the notes on a book. And naturally to leaf through, look again at the engravings, touch the paper that still goes crack crack under one's fingers, while e-books do not respond to the touch.
quotes.text_it: Il piacere di un bibliofilo è quello di compulsare cataloghi, di fare collazioni, di aggiornare continuamente le notizie su un libro. E naturalmente di sfogliare, rivedere le incisioni, toccare la carta che fa ancora crac crac sotto le dita, mentre gli e-books non reagiscono al tatto.
quotes.source: Umberto Eco, from the essay 'Collazioni di un collezionista', as quoted in 'Il mondo di Eco in una stanza', Corriere del Ticino, 26 June 2022
quotes.speaker: Umberto Eco
quotes.context: The same essay is the source of 'se per avere un libro non ha compiuto un sacrificio, non c'è piacere della conquista'.

quotes.text: my personal 'Bibliotheca Semiologica Curiosa, Lunatica, Magica et Pneumatica,' which has been a mainstay to me in the present endeavor.
quotes.source: Umberto Eco, The Search for the Perfect Language, trans. James Fentress (Oxford: Blackwell, 1995), acknowledgements, pp. 5–6
quotes.speaker: Umberto Eco
quotes.context: Earliest printed use of the name found; Eco there says the passion for 'old books on imaginary, artificial, mad and occult languages' began with a copy of Wilkins's Essay towards a Real Character bought in 1983.

quotes.text: As a scholar I am interested in the philosophy of language, semiotics, call it what you want, and one of the main features of the human language is the possibility of lying. A dog doesn't lie. When it barks, it means there is somebody outside. […] From lies to forgeries the step is not so long, and I have written technical essays on the logic of forgeries and on the influence of forgeries on history. The most famous and terrible of those forgeries is the Protocols.
quotes.source: Stephen Moss, 'Umberto Eco: "People are tired of simple things. They want to be challenged"', The Guardian, 27 November 2011
quotes.speaker: Umberto Eco
quotes.context: Same article: 'His two libraries, at the homes he shares with his German-born wife Renate Ramge in Milan and Rimini, contain 50,000 books, including 1,200 rare titles' and 'He has called books "the corridors of the mind"'.

quotes.text: The room of the ancients was from the start Umberto's refuge, without telephone, without computer, with the scores and his flutes, which he played almost every day. […] Umberto was proud of the rarity of many of his purchases, and showed them to family and to the few friends admitted to the room with the pride and the smile of the passionate collector. […] To his grandchildren he showed with amusement the animals, monsters and creatures from the books of Aldrovandi and Kircher; to others also Maier's coloured Atalanta fugiens, or the splendid page composition of the Hypnerotomachia Poliphili, printed by Aldus Manutius in 1499.
quotes.text_it: La stanza degli antichi fu da subito il rifugio di Umberto, senza telefono, senza computer, con gli spartiti e i suoi flauti, che suonava quasi ogni giorno. […] Umberto era fiero della rarità di molti dei suoi acquisti, e li mostrava ai familiari e ai pochi amici ammessi nella stanza con l'orgoglio e il sorriso del collezionista appassionato. […] Ai nipoti mostrava con divertimento gli animali, i mostri e le creature dai libri di Aldrovandi e Kircher, agli altri anche l'Atalanta fugiens colorata di Meyer [Maier], o la splendida composizione delle pagine della Hypnerotomachia Poliphili, stampata da Aldo Manuzio nel 1499.
quotes.source: ANSA, 'Lo studiolo di Umberto Eco alla Biblioteca Braidense apre per la prima volta al pubblico', 4 May 2022; also Fondazione Umberto Eco, 'Le biblioteche', and Rivista Studio, 8 May 2022
quotes.speaker: Renate Ramge, Carlotta Eco and Stefano Eco (joint statement)
quotes.context: Family description of the Stanza degli antichi, which the Braidense 'Studiolo Umberto Eco' (open since 5 May 2022) reproduces in size and atmosphere; the original room was elliptical, the Braidense one rectangular (Rivista Studio).

quotes.text: He wanted his rare books to stay in Milan, and to come to the library. […] In his home the rare books were privileged, and placed separately from his modern library.
quotes.text_it: Lui voleva che i suoi libri rari rimanessero a Milano, e venissero in biblioteca. […] A casa sua, i libri rari erano privilegiati, e posizionati separatamente rispetto alla sua biblioteca moderna.
quotes.source: ANSA, 'Alla Braidense collezione di libri antichi di Umberto Eco', 1 February 2021
quotes.speaker: James M. Bradburne (director, Pinacoteca di Brera and Biblioteca Nazionale Braidense)
quotes.context: Announcement of the state acquisition (1,200 editions, 36 incunabula, 380 volumes 16th–19th c.).

quotes.text: When people talk about my father's books they often throw numbers around. Because the libraries are more than one and the total changes depending on how you count them. We can say that in total there are about 43 thousand. […] My father never threw anything away. And that was our ruin.
quotes.text_it: Quando si parla dei libri di mio padre spesso si danno i numeri. Perché le biblioteche sono più d'una e il totale cambia a seconda di come li si conta. Possiamo dire che in totale sono circa 43mila. […] Mio padre non buttava via niente. Ed è stata questa la nostra rovina.
quotes.source: Domani (editorialedomani.it), 2026, 'Le sfide di Domani' event at Fondazione Feltrinelli, Milan
quotes.speaker: Carlotta Eco
quotes.context: Family's reconciliation of the figures: c. 33,000 Milan + c. 11,000 Monte Cerignone = c. 44,000 working library (Fondazione), plus c. 1,300 rare books.

quotes.text: And, my collection concerns only... fake books -- books that say the contrary of...
quotes.source: Writer Umberto Eco: I Was Always Narrating | Louisiana Channel
quotes.speaker: Umberto Eco

quotes.text: I'm afraid that, by now, it might actually be 50,000 books. When my secretary wanted to catalogue them, I asked her not to. My interests change constantly, and so does my library. By the way, if you constantly change your interests, your library will constantly be saying something different about you. Besides, even without a catalogue, I'm forced to remember my books. I have a hallway for literature that's 70 meters long. I walk through it several times a day, and I feel good when I do. Culture isn't knowing when Napoleon died. Culture means knowing how I can find out in two minutes.
quotes.source: 'We Like Lists Because We Don't Want to Die', SPIEGEL interview with Umberto Eco by Susanne Beyer and Lothar Gorris, Spiegel Online International, 11 November 2009
quotes.speaker: Umberto Eco
quotes.context: Answer to 'you have a library of 30,000 volumes. It probably doesn't work without a list or catalogue.' Page fetched directly with curl (spiegel.de blocks WebFetch). Research placement: 'corridoio (bookcase A, literatures)'.

quotes.text: The extra life one gains by reading does not discriminate between great works of art and entertainment literature: don't let yourselves be blackmailed by those who tell you that one must read only important books. I have intense and beautiful memories even of books that were perhaps silly, but which fed long afternoons of excitement.
quotes.text_it: Quel tanto di vita che si conquista leggendo non discrimina tra grandi opere d'arte e letteratura di trattenimento: non fatevi ricattare da chi vi dice che bisogna leggere solo i libri importanti. Ho ricordi intensi e bellissimi anche di libri forse sciocchi, ma che mi hanno nutrito lunghi pomeriggi di eccitazione.
quotes.source: Davide Ferrario (dir.), 'Umberto Eco. La biblioteca del mondo' (Rossofuoco / Fandango, 2022, 80 min), Italian auto-captions of the unofficial upload (caption time 00:34:06)
quotes.speaker: Umberto Eco
quotes.context: Eco text read in the film (an actor's reading of an Eco essay on why reading lengthens life); the sentence 'Non fatevi ricattare…' is the line most reviews quote (giovanniguarino.net). Caption 'sciiti' = 'sciocchi'. Research placement: 'corridoio (bookcase A: feuilleton and comics)'.

quotes.text: The volumes are in Milan, in the house designed expressly to receive them more than thirty years ago: a large ring-shaped apartment in whose corridors, on specially reinforced floors, the bookcases were mounted. Following the path traced by the long full-height shelves – Italian and foreign literature, poetry, popular and genre fiction, feuilleton, comics, literary history and criticism, the press, communication and mass media, art and iconology – one reaches Umberto Eco's large study, with bookcases of a complex comb-and-island structure holding volumes on philosophy, science, history, philology, mnemonics, puzzles, publishing, linguistics and semiotics, besides the books by and about Eco.
quotes.text_it: I volumi si trovano a Milano, nella casa disegnata appositamente per accoglierli, oltre trent'anni fa: un grande appartamento a forma di anello nei cui corridoi, dal pavimento appositamente rinforzato, vennero montate le librerie. Seguendo la strada tracciata dai lunghi scaffali a tutta altezza – letteratura italiana e straniera, poesia, narrativa popolare e di genere, feuilleton, fumetto, storia e critica letteraria, stampa, comunicazione e mass media, arte e iconologia – si giunge al grande studio di Umberto Eco, con biblioteche dalla complessa struttura a pettine e isola che ospitano volumi relativi a filosofia, scienza, storia, filologia, mnemotecniche, enigmistica, editoria, linguistica e semiotica, oltre ai libri di e su Eco.
quotes.source: Fondazione Umberto Eco, 'Le biblioteche' (fondazioneumbertoeco.org/lebiblioteche), Italian text; English version fetched directly
quotes.speaker: Fondazione Umberto Eco
quotes.context: The institutional description of the route corridor -> study, and the key for the lettered bookcases (A corridor literatures and comics; B Jewish thought/magic/Kabbalah/Joyce; C books on books; D esotericism/encyclopedism/alchemy; E ancient art; F aesthetics/photography; G architecture/design/labyrinths; H contemporary art/theatre/music; I ancient and Christian philosophy; L medieval–modern philosophy; M continental philosophy and Eco; N translation/dictionaries/philosophy of science; O encyclopedias/semiotics; P text theory/semiotics/logic; Q Eco in 40 languages; R, S psychology/sociology/anthropology). Research placement: 'corridoio (A) -> studio (B–S)'.

quotes.text: In the house in Piazza Castello the books were laid out horizontally, along a very long corridor. This made it possible to line up the series of the literatures – Italian, English, German – and everything converged at the centre of this corridor where the feuilletons were. […] A whole series of crossings branched off, between the learned and the popular. And these routes changed continually, according to his research.
quotes.text_it: Nella casa di Piazza Castello i libri erano disposti in orizzontale, su un lunghissimo corridoio. Questo consentiva di allineare le serie delle letterature – italiana, inglese, tedesca – e tutto confluiva nel centro di questo corridoio dove c'erano i feuilleton. […] Si diramavano tutta una serie di incroci, tra il colto e l'inclito. E questi percorsi cambiavano di continuo, a seconda delle sue ricerche.
quotes.source: 'Umberto Eco, l'eredità dei libri e delle biblioteche: a Bologna una nuova casa per la sua collezione', Domani (editorialedomani.it), 2026, report of the event 'Le sfide di Domani' at Fondazione Feltrinelli, Milan
quotes.speaker: Riccardo Fedriga (Università di Bologna; Fondazione Umberto Eco)
quotes.context: Explains the corridor as a set of parallel literary time-lines meeting at the feuilleton section in the middle — the layout Bologna reproduced in its 'stanza delle letterature'. Research placement: 'corridoio (bookcase A)'.

quotes.text: The map untangles itself in the room of the literatures. Italian, French, Anglo-Saxon, German, Central European, Slavic, Hispano-American and many more. All of these are laid out along time-lines that can be read horizontally, diachronically. If we take English literature, for instance, one can start consulting from the Arthurian cycle to T.S. Eliot. […] The time-lines, then, on reaching the nineteenth century, develop in various directions, intersecting with the genres, such as crime and science fiction, popular literature and the feuilleton.
quotes.text_it: La mappa si sgroviglia nella stanza delle letterature. Quella italiana, francese, anglosassone, tedesca, mitteleuropea, slava, ispano-americana e tante altre ancora. Tutte queste sono disposte lungo linee temporali che possono essere lette in orizzontale, in senso diacronico. Se prendiamo la letteratura inglese, per esempio, si può iniziare a consultare dal ciclo arturiano a T.S. Eliot. […] Le linee del tempo, poi, giunti nell'Ottocento, si sviluppano in varie direzioni intersecandosi con i generi, come il giallo e la fantascienza, la letteratura popolare e il feuilleton.
quotes.source: 'Inaugurata la Biblioteca Eco. Un viaggio di 32mila volumi nell'universo creato dal prof', Il Resto del Carlino (Bologna), 2 July 2026
quotes.speaker: Amalia Apicella (journalist, Il Resto del Carlino)
quotes.context: Description of how the Milan corridor time-lines were rebuilt in Bologna; the same article: 'La disposizione segue la regola del buon vicino… i volumi non seguono un ordine alfabetico o un rigido indice tematico, ma le relazioni interdisciplinari'. Research placement: 'corridoio (bookcase A) as rebuilt in Bologna'.

film_notes.description: Very long straight corridor (~20 m, ~1.6 m wide) lined with white full-height shelving 11 shelves high on the right-hand side for its whole length (Fondazione bookcase A, 25 bays). In the first third the left wall is shelved too (both sides shelves, film 62-70 s); for the rest the left wall is plain with a row of small framed prints/plexiglass frames. A sliding ladder on a rail and a folding stepladder stand in the corridor. Ceiling with recessed spots; carpeted floor (beige) in the corridor, parquet elsewhere. At the far end a tall French window with vertical iron bars (balcony door), a radiator beneath it, a small metal waste-bin, a wall spotlight above the door.
film_notes.note: 20.8 x 1.6 m box; shelves right (25 bays x 0.8 m); left wall: shelves for bays 1-7, prints for the rest; balcony door at the far end; door into the study on the left ~1.5 m before the end.

film_notes.item: Corridor end lobby by the balcony door
film_notes.description: The last 2 m of the long corridor: on the left a plain wall with a small speckled grey abstract canvas (~50 x 70 cm) and a switch plate; ahead the French window with vertical bars and a low radiator, a wall lamp above; to the right the last bays of case A. The study door opens on the left just here (Eco turns left at film 82 s / Hq66 329 s).
film_notes.note: Place the balcony door on the corridor end wall; door to study on the left wall 1-2 m before it.

film_notes.description: Beige carpet-like floor in the corridor and vestibule (parquet in salotto, study and rare room); flat white ceiling with a line of recessed spots; skirting-height sockets; the corridor ceiling is lower than the rooms.
film_notes.note: Corridor floor beige, rooms light oak parquet; ceiling white.

quotes.text: If I had to tell the story of my father's library I would start here: these are the feuilletons, the nineteenth-century serial novels he read as a boy and partly read to us too; and here are the beautiful engravings of the period, which he then used so much, above all in the novels, in The Prague Cemetery. … Here there is a marker: all of French literature stretches along this line, and here too; while below, for example, there is Italian literature, and if we go upwards instead we still stay within popular literature and arrive at the comics.
quotes.text_it: Se dovessi raccontare la biblioteca di mio padre inizierei da qua: sono i feuilleton, i romanzi d'appendice dell'Ottocento che lui ha letto da ragazzo e che in parte ha letto anche a noi; e qui si trovano le immagini bellissime degli incisori del periodo, che lui poi ha utilizzato tantissimo, soprattutto nei romanzi, nel Cimitero di Praga. … Qui c'è un segnale: si estende un po' tutta la letteratura francese lungo questa linea, e anche qua; mentre qui sotto, ad esempio, c'è la letteratura italiana, e se andiamo invece verso l'alto rimaniamo sempre nell'ambito della letteratura popolare e arriviamo fino ai fumetti.
quotes.source: Umberto Eco. La biblioteca del mondo (Davide Ferrario, 2022)
quotes.speaker: Carlotta Eco

quotes.text: This working library is organised by sector, yes, but not alphabetically, rather by sub-sectors, where things then got moved around: almost only he knew where to find the books, because it was a living thing, not an archive, not a library codified in the classical sense.
quotes.text_it: Questa biblioteca di lavoro è sì organizzata per settori, ma non alfabeticamente, piuttosto per sottosettori, dove poi alcune cose venivano spostate: lo sapeva quasi solo lui dove trovare i libri, perché era una cosa viva, non era un archivio, non era una biblioteca codificata nel senso classico.
quotes.source: Umberto Eco. La biblioteca del mondo (Davide Ferrario, 2022)
quotes.speaker: Stefano Eco

quotes.text: This library also has its own scent, a smell, and a sound too, I would say, because when you move through those corridors full of books everything is muffled: I feel very protected in there.
quotes.text_it: Questa biblioteca ha anche un suo profumo, un odore, e anche un suono, direi, perché quando ti muovi in quei corridoi pieni di libri tutto è più attutito: io mi sento molto protetta lì in mezzo.
quotes.source: Umberto Eco. La biblioteca del mondo (Davide Ferrario, 2022)
quotes.speaker: Carlotta Eco
quotes.context: Spoken over the corridor shots from 51:04; the speaker is on camera in the study from 51:15 as the sentence ends (the Italian 'protetta' is feminine).

quotes.text: Since my library holds fifty thousand volumes, the unhappy man only tries to bring forward the moment of farewell, pleading sudden engagements. What the unhappy man does not know is that the library is not only the place of your memory, where you keep what you have read, but the place of universal memory, where one day, at the fatal moment, you will be able to find what others have read before you. It is a repository where, at the limit, everything blurs together and generates a vertigo, a cocktail of learned memory.
quotes.text_it: Visto che la mia biblioteca conta cinquantamila volumi, l'infelice cerca soltanto di anticipare il momento del commiato, adducendo improvvisi impegni. Quello che l'infelice non sa è che la biblioteca non è solo il luogo della tua memoria, dove conservi quel che hai letto, ma il luogo della memoria universale, dove un giorno, nel momento fatale, potrai trovare quello che altri hanno letto prima di te. È un repositorio dove al limite tutto si confonde e genera una vertigine, un cocktail della memoria dotta.
quotes.source: Umberto Eco, lectio magistralis at the Fiera Internazionale del Libro di Torino, May 2007 (published as 'La memoria vegetale', in La memoria vegetale e altri scritti di bibliofilia, Rovello 2007 / Bompiani 2011)
quotes.speaker: Umberto Eco
quotes.context: Continuation of q04. Widely quoted in the 2026 Bologna coverage (zero.eu) together with 'Una biblioteca non è una somma di libri – è un organismo vivente con una vita autonoma'.

quotes.text: A library is not a sum of books – it is a living organism with a life of its own […] The library is not only the place of your memory, where you keep what you have read, but the place of universal memory, a repository where at the limit everything blurs together and generates a vertigo, a cocktail of learned memory.
quotes.text_it: Una biblioteca non è una somma di libri – è un organismo vivente con una vita autonoma […] La biblioteca non è solo il luogo della tua memoria, dove conservi quel che hai letto, ma il luogo della memoria universale, un repositorio dove al limite tutto si confonde e genera una vertigine, un cocktail della memoria dotta.
quotes.source: Umberto Eco, lectio magistralis at the Fiera Internazionale del Libro di Torino, May 2007 (published as 'La memoria vegetale', in La memoria vegetale e altri scritti di bibliofilia, Rovello 2007 / Bompiani 2011) — as quoted in Zero.eu, 'A Bologna apre la Biblioteca Eco: 32mila libri, nello stesso ordine in cui li aveva lasciati il professore', July 2026
quotes.speaker: Umberto Eco
quotes.context: The 'organismo vivente' opening sentence could only be found in secondary quotation (Zero.eu, AIB Notizie); the second sentence matches q05 verbatim.

quotes.text: I don't go to the bookshelves to choose a book to read. I go to the bookshelves to pick up a book I know I need in that moment. It's a different story. For instance, if you were to ask me about contemporary authors, I would look through my collections of Roth or DeLillo to remember exactly what I loved. I am a scholar. In a way I should say I am never freely choosing. I am following the needs of the job I am doing at any given time.
quotes.source: Lila Azam Zanganeh, 'Umberto Eco, The Art of Fiction No. 197', The Paris Review 185 (Summer 2008)
quotes.speaker: Umberto Eco
quotes.context: Answer to 'With so many volumes, when you go to the bookshelf, how do you decide which book to pick up and read?'

quotes.text: The apartment is a labyrinth of corridors lined with bookcases that reach all the way up to extraordinarily high ceilings—thirty thousand volumes, said Eco, with another twenty thousand at his manor. I saw scientific treatises by Ptolemy and novels by Calvino, critical studies of Saussure and Joyce, entire sections devoted to medieval history and arcane manuscripts. The library feels alive, as many of the books seem worn from heavy use; Eco reads at great speed and has a prodigious memory. In his study, a maze of shelves contains Eco's own complete works in all their translations (Arabic, Finnish, Japanese . . . I lost count after more than thirty languages).
quotes.source: Lila Azam Zanganeh, 'Umberto Eco, The Art of Fiction No. 197', The Paris Review 185 (Summer 2008)
quotes.speaker: Lila Azam Zanganeh (interviewer)
quotes.context: Eyewitness description, August 2007; the living room had 'several glass cases displaying seashells and rare comics, a lute, a collection of recorders' and the Castello Sforzesco visible through the windows. Research placement: 'corridoio / studio (bookcase Q for translations)'.

quotes.text: One of the misunderstandings that dominate the notion of a library is that one goes to the library to look for a book whose title one knows. In truth it often happens that one goes to the library because one wants a book whose title one knows, but the main function of the library, at least the function of the library in my own house and of any friend's we may go to visit, is to discover books whose existence one did not suspect, and which nevertheless turn out to be of extreme importance to us. Now, it is true that this discovery can come from leafing through the catalogue, but there is nothing more revealing and exciting than exploring shelves that perhaps gather all the books on a certain subject, something one could not have discovered in the author catalogue, and finding next to the book one went looking for another book, which one had not gone looking for, but which turns out to be fundamental. That is, the ideal function of a library is to be a bit like the bouquiniste's stall, something in which one makes trouvailles, and this function can only be allowed by free access to the corridors of the shelves.
quotes.text_it: uno dei malintesi che dominano la nozione di biblioteca è che si vada in biblioteca per cercare un libro di cui si conosce il titolo. In verità accade sovente di andare in biblioteca perché si vuole un libro di cui si conosce il titolo, ma la principale funzione della biblioteca, almeno la funzione della biblioteca di casa mia e di qualsiasi amico che possiamo andare a visitare, è di scoprire dei libri di cui non si sospettava l'esistenza, e che tuttavia si scoprono essere di estrema importanza per noi. Ora, è vero che questa scoperta può essere data sfogliando il catalogo, ma non c'è niente di più rivelativo e appassionante dell'esplorare degli scaffali che magari riuniscono tutti i libri di un certo argomento, cosa che intanto sul catalogo per autore non si sarebbe potuto scoprire, e trovare accanto al libro che si era andati a cercare un altro libro, che non si era andati a cercare, ma che si rivela come fondamentale. Cioè, la funzione ideale di una biblioteca è di essere un po' come la bancarella del bouquiniste, qualcosa in cui si fanno delle trouvailles, e questa funzione può essere permessa solo dalla libera accessibilità ai corridoi degli scaffali.
quotes.source: Umberto Eco, De Bibliotheca, lecture given 10 March 1981 at Palazzo Sormani for the 25th anniversary of the Biblioteca Comunale di Milano (Milano: Biblioteca Comunale, 'I quaderni di Palazzo Sormani', 1981; repr. in Sette anni di desiderio, Bompiani 1983)
quotes.speaker: Umberto Eco
quotes.context: The source of the popular paraphrase 'a library is a place where you go to find books you didn't know you needed'; note 'la biblioteca di casa mia' and the subject-shelving argument that explains his own arrangement.

quotes.text: A big house can give the impression of the literary humanist living cut off from the world. The house is big precisely because otherwise the books would not fit: from the previous one I was evicted with the help of the civil engineering office, because it seemed the bookcases would bring the walls down.
quotes.text_it: Una grande casa può dare l'impressione dell'umanista letterato che vive così appartato dal mondo. La casa è grande appunto perché i libri altrimenti non ci stanno: in quella precedente sono stato sfrattato con concorso del genio civile, perché pareva che le librerie facessero crollare i muri.
quotes.source: Davide Ferrario (dir.), 'Umberto Eco. La biblioteca del mondo' (Rossofuoco / Fandango, 2022, 80 min), Italian auto-captions of the unofficial upload (caption time 00:08:40)
quotes.speaker: Umberto Eco
quotes.context: Archival interview used in the film; the official English subtitles of the clip ygvl-_gtAP8 (00:00:44–00:01:02) render it 'The house is big otherwise I wouldn't know where to put the books. I was evicted from the last one after an inspection by the city engineers because they were afraid the floors would collapse.' Auto-caption 'collare' corrected to 'crollare'.

quotes.text: We, insofar as we can say "I", are our memory, that is, memory is the soul. If someone totally loses his memory he becomes a vegetable and no longer has a soul. […] Collective memory is collective identity. […] There is a counterpart of individual memory, which is the vegetal memory of the library: the sum of all libraries is the sum of humanity's memory.
quotes.text_it: Noi, nella misura in cui possiamo dire "io", siamo la nostra memoria, cioè la memoria è l'anima. Se uno perde totalmente la memoria diventa un vegetale e non ha più l'anima. […] La memoria collettiva è l'identità collettiva. […] C'è un corrispettivo della memoria individuale che è la memoria vegetale della biblioteca: l'insieme delle biblioteche è l'insieme della memoria dell'umanità.
quotes.source: Davide Ferrario (dir.), 'Umberto Eco. Sulla memoria. Una conversazione in tre parti' (video installation for the Venice Art Biennale, 2015), Italian auto-captions, part 1 (caption times 00:00:43, 00:03:08, 00:03:25)
quotes.speaker: Umberto Eco
quotes.context: Narration of the Biennale installation; the walk through the corridors starts around 00:04:54 (music only) after 'la biblioteca delle biblioteche' at 00:04:50.

rooms.name: The big study
rooms.blurb: Reached at the end of the corridors: "il grande studio di Umberto Eco, con biblioteche dalla complessa struttura a pettine e isola" holding philosophy, science, history, philology, mnemonics, puzzles, publishing, linguistics and semiotics, and the books by and on Eco (fondazione-lebiblioteche). Behind the desk the working tools (dictionaries, lexica); one whole wall of philosophy from the Presocratics, the opposite side semiotics, linguistics and literary theory; his own works in 60+ languages on the right and books about him at the far right (criticaletteraria-2022, zanni-2010); a black round table, sliding ladders and a black sofa appear in the 2011 and 2022 photographs (getty-2011, criticaletteraria-2022).

film_notes.description: Large bright room (~14 x 10 m) with white full-height shelving on every wall plus low island bookcases ('pettine e isola') standing in the middle; two white 3-blade ceiling fans; recessed ceiling spots; windows along one long wall (French windows with shutters onto an internal terrace with planters); radiators under the windows; parquet floor. Furniture: L-shaped black desk with computer, printer and phone by the windows; 2-3 black mesh office chairs; a black round pedestal table (~1.4 m dia) at the window end; black leather two-seater sofa; black leather armchair; sliding ladders on rails; black wheeled filing cabinet; white cupboards under the islands; framed caricature portraits of Eco and framed drawings on the pillars between windows; a white door with notes pinned on it on the far wall (where Eco takes a book in the 2015 walk).
film_notes.note: Box 14 x 10 m; window wall opposite the corridor door; islands run perpendicular to the long wall; desk in the corner nearest the corridor door by the windows; round table at the far end by the windows.

film_notes.item: Internal terrace with planters (outside the study windows)
film_notes.description: An outdoor terrace/loggia along the study's window wall: a row of terracotta planters with pansies and bergenias on the parapet, ivy climbing the wall, a drainpipe, an air-conditioner unit; through one window the dictionary shelves (LE ROBERT spines = Fondazione Nb 'Dictionaries') and a pendant lamp; through an open French window tall shelves with a sliding ladder and a low bookcase with piles.
film_notes.note: Optional exterior: a 1.5 m deep terrace outside the study windows with 6-8 planters; helps locate the study on the courtyard side.

film_notes.description: Two white three-blade ceiling fans on rods and a grid of recessed halogen spots in the study ceiling.
