quotes.text: This is my father's study, in the house he and my mother chose thirty years ago so that his whole book collection could be kept: the 1,200 old books and the 30,000 modern ones.
quotes.text_it: Qui siamo nello studio di mio padre, dentro la casa che lui e mia madre hanno scelto trent'anni fa per poter tenere tutta la collezione di libri di mio padre, cioè i 1.200 libri antichi e i 30.000 libri moderni.
quotes.source: Umberto Eco. La biblioteca del mondo (Davide Ferrario, 2022)
quotes.speaker: Stefano Eco

quotes.text: The flat is big precisely because otherwise the books would not fit: I was evicted from the previous one, with the civil engineers involved, because the bookcases seemed to be bringing the walls down.
quotes.text_it: La casa è grande appunto perché i libri altrimenti non ci stanno: da quella precedente sono stato sfrattato, con un concorso del Genio civile, perché pareva che le librerie facessero crollare i muri.
quotes.source: Umberto Eco. La biblioteca del mondo (Davide Ferrario, 2022)
quotes.speaker: Umberto Eco

quotes.text: My secretary once wanted to draw up a catalogue of my books so that she knew exactly where each one was. I persuaded her not to. While I was writing The Search for the Perfect Language I looked at my library anew, with new criteria, and changed it around. Which books would best nourish my thoughts on the subject? When I finished writing, some books went back on the linguistics shelf, and some to aesthetics, but others were already being used for a new piece of research.
quotes.source: Umberto Eco and Jean-Claude Carrière, This Is Not the End of the Book (conversation curated by Jean-Philippe de Tonnac, trans. Polly McLean, Harvill Secker, London 2011; orig. N'espérez pas vous débarrasser des livres, 2009 / Non sperate di liberarvi dei libri, Bompiani 2009), chapter on organising a library
quotes.speaker: Umberto Eco
quotes.context: Direct testimony that the shelves were re-sorted by research project; Carrière replies that 'if you classified by subject, you'd have books by someone like Kircher on every shelf'.

quotes.text: The list is the origin of culture. It's part of the history of art and literature. What does culture want? To make infinity comprehensible. It also wants to create order — not always, but often. And how, as a human being, does one face infinity? How does one attempt to grasp the incomprehensible? Through lists, through catalogs, through collections in museums and through encyclopedias and dictionaries.
quotes.source: 'We Like Lists Because We Don't Want to Die', SPIEGEL interview with Umberto Eco by Susanne Beyer and Lothar Gorris, Spiegel Online International, 11 November 2009
quotes.speaker: Umberto Eco
quotes.context: Opening answer of the interview about the Louvre exhibition 'Vertige de la liste' (2009).

quotes.text: We have a limit, a very discouraging, humiliating limit: death. That's why we like all the things that we assume have no limits and, therefore, no end. It's a way of escaping thoughts about death. We like lists because we don't want to die.
quotes.source: 'We Like Lists Because We Don't Want to Die', SPIEGEL interview with Umberto Eco by Susanne Beyer and Lothar Gorris, Spiegel Online International, 11 November 2009
quotes.speaker: Umberto Eco
quotes.context: The sentence that gave the interview its title.

quotes.text: The list doesn't destroy culture; it creates it. Wherever you look in cultural history, you will find lists. In fact, there is a dizzying array: lists of saints, armies and medicinal plants, or of treasures and book titles. Think of the nature collections of the 16th century. My novels, by the way, are full of lists.
quotes.source: 'We Like Lists Because We Don't Want to Die', SPIEGEL interview with Umberto Eco by Susanne Beyer and Lothar Gorris, Spiegel Online International, 11 November 2009
quotes.speaker: Umberto Eco
quotes.context: 'Lists of book titles' and Wunderkammern: the same logic as his own catalogues and the mirabilia in the Stanza degli antichi.

quotes.text: We have three types of memory. The first one is organic, which is the memory made of flesh and blood and the one administrated by our brain. The second is mineral […] this second type is also the electronic memory of today's computers, based upon silicon. We have also known another kind of memory, the vegetal one, the one represented by the first papyruses […] and then on books, made of paper. […] Libraries, over the centuries, have been the most important way of keeping our collective wisdom. They were and still are a sort of universal brain where we can retrieve what we have forgotten and what we still do not know. If you will allow me to use such a metaphor, a library is the best possible imitation, by human beings, of a divine mind, where the whole universe is viewed and understood at the same time.
quotes.source: Umberto Eco, 'Vegetal and Mineral Memory: The Future of Books', lecture delivered at the Bibliotheca Alexandrina, 1 November 2003 (published by the Bibliotheca Alexandrina, 2003; Italian version in La memoria vegetale)
quotes.speaker: Umberto Eco
quotes.context: The 'vegetal memory' definition in Eco's own English; the lecture ends 'Long life to this temple of vegetal memory.'

quotes.text: We are temporal beings, we live in time: without memory one does not build, one does not plan one's own future.
quotes.text_it: Noi siamo esseri temporali, viviamo nel tempo: senza memoria non si costruisce, non si progetta il proprio futuro.
quotes.source: Davide Ferrario (dir.), 'Umberto Eco. La biblioteca del mondo' (Rossofuoco / Fandango, 2022, 80 min), Italian auto-captions of the unofficial upload (caption time 00:11:08)
quotes.speaker: Umberto Eco
quotes.context: From the 2015 'Sulla memoria' material reused in the film (cf. zj1kwT87ne0 00:04:02–00:04:53: 'Senza memoria non c'è anima. Per proiettarci sul futuro bisogna avere un'anima').

quotes.text: Perhaps you have read that story by Borges with a character called Funes the Memorious, who remembers everything […] he has a total memory and is practically an imbecile, because he cannot cope. It is like the web: if we suddenly had to know everything that is on the web we would go mad. So what is the second virtue of memory? The first is the one that preserves, the second is the one that filters. Woe if memory, individual as well as collective, did not carry out decimations day by day, throwing away what is not worth keeping.
quotes.text_it: Forse voi avete letto quella novella di Borges dove c'è un personaggio che si chiama Funes il memorioso, che ricorda tutto […] ha una memoria totale ed è praticamente un imbecille, perché non ce la fa. È come il web: se noi dovessimo di colpo sapere tutto quello che c'è nel web diventeremmo pazzi. Quindi qual è la seconda virtù della memoria? La prima è quella che conserva, la seconda è quella che filtra. Guai se la memoria, sia individuale che collettiva, non facesse delle decimazioni giorno per giorno, buttasse via quello che non vale la pena.
quotes.source: Davide Ferrario (dir.), 'Umberto Eco. La biblioteca del mondo' (Rossofuoco / Fandango, 2022, 80 min), Italian auto-captions of the unofficial upload (caption time 00:22:51)
quotes.speaker: Umberto Eco
quotes.context: Memory as selection; the library as a filtered memory rather than an archive of everything. Caption 'filica' read as 'filtra' (context).

quotes.text: I went home and started jotting down a list of monks' names, and then I wrote to a chemist friend asking how one can poison a person while he is reading a book. He answered me, then I destroyed the letter.
quotes.text_it: Sono tornato a casa e ho cominciato a buttar giù una lista di nomi di monaci, e poi ho scritto a un amico chimico come si può avvelenare una persona mentre legge un libro. Lui mi ha risposto, poi ho distrutto la lettera.
quotes.source: Davide Ferrario (dir.), 'Umberto Eco. La biblioteca del mondo' (Rossofuoco / Fandango, 2022, 80 min), Italian auto-captions of the unofficial upload (caption time 00:48:33)
quotes.speaker: Umberto Eco
quotes.context: Origin of The Name of the Rose told as a list; same anecdote in the Paris Review ('making a list of names of fictional medieval monks') and the Louisiana interview (M8IWTOFNlOc 00:03:05).

quotes.text: The list has always fascinated me. Does the list have something to do with memory? Well yes, because it is a way of gathering everything that was known about something without being obliged to organise it. The first list begins with the catalogue of ships in the Iliad: Homer cannot express the greatness, the strength, the immensity of the Achaean army that is landing, and he makes a list, a list of the ships.
quotes.text_it: La lista mi ha sempre affascinato. Ha la lista qualche cosa a che vedere con la memoria? Ma sì, perché è un modo di raccogliere tutto quello che si sapeva a proposito di qualcosa senza essere obbligati ad organizzarlo. Il primo elenco comincia col catalogo delle navi nell'Iliade: Omero non riesce ad esprimere la grandezza, la forza, l'immensità dell'esercito acheo che sta sbarcando, e fa un elenco, un elenco delle navi.
quotes.source: Davide Ferrario (dir.), 'Umberto Eco. Sulla memoria. Una conversazione in tre parti' (video installation for the Venice Art Biennale, 2015), Italian auto-captions, part 3 (caption time 00:03:11)
quotes.speaker: Umberto Eco
quotes.context: Lists as unorganised memory — the same argument as The Infinity of Lists (2009) and the Spiegel interview; caption 'AEO' = 'acheo'.

quotes.text: Without memory there is no soul. To project ourselves onto the future we must have a soul.
quotes.text_it: Senza memoria non c'è anima. Per proiettarci sul futuro bisogna avere un'anima.
quotes.source: Davide Ferrario (dir.), 'Umberto Eco. Sulla memoria. Una conversazione in tre parti' (video installation for the Venice Art Biennale, 2015), Italian auto-captions, part 2 (caption time 00:04:47)
quotes.speaker: Umberto Eco
quotes.context: Preceded by 'siamo come l'atleta che per fare un balzo avanti deve fare sempre un passo indietro' (00:04:07).

quotes.text: Bought, my foot! They send them to me, that's why it can't be stopped…
quotes.text_it: Macché comprati! Me li mandano, è per questo che non si può fermare…
quotes.source: Andrea Zanni, 'Intervista a Umberto Eco per WMI' (Wikimedia Italia), aubreymcfato.com, 13 May 2010 — visit to the Milan flat, 24 April 2010
quotes.speaker: Umberto Eco
quotes.context: Answer to 'did you buy them all?'. Zanni's layout notes: 'La libreria nel lunghissimo corridoio è solo la narrativa, mentre la grande stanza contiene … sulla destra un'intera libreria di libri scritti da lui e tradotti in ogni lingua; sull'estrema destra vari scaffali di libri scritti su di lui; una parte centrale con la sezione dei cretini (Dumézil e Zolla…); il cimitero, una serie di foto di Eco con Montale, Moravia, Foucault'; rare-book room 'stanzino adibito, tutto in legno, un'enorme lente sul tavolo'.

quotes.text: Eco catalogued by sympathy, by intellectual affinity.
quotes.text_it: Eco catalogava per simpatia, per affinità intellettuale.
quotes.source: 'Un pomeriggio nella casa-biblioteca di Umberto Eco. Cronaca di un'esperienza mistica. O quasi', CriticaLetteraria, November 2022 (visit guided by Carlotta Eco and Mario Andreose)
quotes.speaker: Carlotta Eco (as reported by CriticaLetteraria)
quotes.context: Reported phrase, not a full sentence in quotation marks. The article's room sequence: salotto (art books, encyclopaedias, atlases, the vetrina of current research) -> vestibolo (Joyce shelf; Kabbalah, mystery, magic, Templars, devil, alchemy) -> corridoio (the 'bosco narrativo': Italian and French authors at eye level from Dante to today; comics on the top and bottom shelves) -> studio (dictionaries behind the desk; one wall philosophy from the Presocratics; opposite side semiotics, linguistics, theory of literature; Eco's works in 60+ languages and books about him).

quotes.text: The most extraordinary thing is that the books keep the exact original arrangement Eco wanted, making the rooms of this library a real laboratory of ideas ranging from medieval philosophy to the classic comics of Linus.
quotes.text_it: La cosa più straordinaria è che i libri conservano l'esatta disposizione originale voluta da Eco, rendendo le sale di questa biblioteca un vero e proprio laboratorio di idee che spazia dalla filosofia medievale ai fumetti classici di Linus.
quotes.source: Artribune, 'A Bologna inaugura la Biblioteca Eco: Palazzo Poggi accoglie oltre 30mila volumi appartenuti a Umberto Eco', July 2026
quotes.speaker: Matteo Lepore (Mayor of Bologna)
quotes.context: Opening of the Biblioteca Eco, Palazzo Poggi (Piazza Puntoni 2), 1 July 2026: 32,000+ volumes in 10 thematic rooms, 600 linear metres of shelving; 'prima del trasferimento, la biblioteca è stata studiata e rilevata scaffale per scaffale'.

objects.description: Black square coffee table (~1.2 x 1.2 m, low) entirely covered by 10-14 stacks of new books and art catalogues, each 6-15 books, 15-35 cm tall, mostly hardbacks with dust jackets, a few large art books; spines face the sofa. Legible covers in 2015: 'Inventing the Enemy' (Eco), 'Имя розы' (Russian Name of the Rose), 'Une image peut en cacher une autre', 'Italia Vostra'; in 2022 Adelphi/Einaudi paperbacks, 'Privati' (?), Deutschland. Two small stacks placed on the coffee table in front of Eco for the 2015 interview: 'Inventing the Enemy' (English, striped cover), 'Имя розы', a French exhibition catalogue 'Une image peut en cacher une autre'.

books.title: Le Relationi vniuersali di Giouanni Botero benese, diuise in sette parti. Alle quali vi sono aggiunte nuouamente i Capitani dell'istesso auttore, con le relationi di Spagna; del Stato della Chiesa, & di Sauoia. Nella prima parte, si contiene la descrittione dell'Europa, dell'Asia, ... Nella seconda, si dà contezza de'maggiori prencipi del mondo; ... Nella terza, si tratta ancor de'popoli d'ogni credenza; cattolici, giudei, gentili, & scismatici. Nella quarta, sitratta delle superstizioni in che viueuano già le genti del mondo nuouo; ... nella quinta, dassi contezza di ciò, che fecero i capitani illustri nella Europa. Nella sesta, discriuonosi le relationi de i Regni di Spagna, e dello Stato della Chiesa. Con le figure e due copiosissime tauole. Inoltre vi s'aggiunge nell'vltima un breue racconto di mostri, vol. 2: Delle relationi vniuersali di Giouanni Botero benese, parte seconda. Nella quale si tratta de'maggiori prencipi, che siano al mondo, & delle cagion
